questions.stem: An 8-month-old girl is brought to the paediatric outpatient department by her mother because of bilateral lower limb and abdomen swelling. Physical examination reveals peripheral oedema and hepatomegaly. On auscultation, a loud systolic ejection murmur is heard in the pulmonary area, and the pulmonic component of S2 is not audible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: An 8-month-old girl is brought to the paediatric outpatient department by her mother because of bilateral lower limb and abdomen swelling. Physical examination reveals peripheral oedema and hepatomegaly. On auscultation, a loud systolic ejection murmur is heard in the pulmonary area, and the pulmonic component of S2 is not audible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Pulmonary valve stenosis: The patient presents with the clinical features of Pulmonary valve stenosis. In this condition, the cusps of the pulmonary valve are deformed , and due to this, during systole, the valve does not open completely. An eccentric outlet may occur due to partially fused valve leaflets and, in severe cases, only a central pinhole opening for the outflow. Right ventricular hypertrophy occurs because of increased right ventricular systolic pressure due to obstruction of blood flow from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery. In severe cases, pressure in the right ventricle may be higher than systemic systolic arterial pressure. In neonates, blood can shunt from right to left atrium via foramen ovale in cases of severe pulmonic stenosis as compliance of right ventricle (RV) is decreased, leading to cyanosis. Development and growth are not affected in mild to moderate stenosis. Peripheral oedema, exercise intolerance, hepatomegaly, and signs of right heart failure, develop in severe stenosis. Large presystolic jugular ‘a‘ wave causes venous pressure elevation. RV parasternal lift and cardiomegaly are present. A loud systolic ejection murmur and harshness accompanied by thrill are audible in the pulmonary area. Incorrect Options: Option A- Coarctation of the aorta: The origin of ductus arteriosus below the left subclavian artery origin is the most common site of coarctation of the aorta. It is a feature of the turner syndrome and may occur together with subaortic stenosis and mitral valve abnormalities called Shone complex. Hypoperfusion and rapid deterioration can occur after the ductus arteriosus in neonates who have coarctation. Patients have high blood pressures in the upper limbs and low blood pressure in the lower limbs. Radio-femoral delay is characteristic. A harsh systolic murmur below the left clavicle may be heard. Prostaglandin E1 infusion is given to prevent the closure of the ductus arteriosus. After stabilisation, surgical repair should be performed. As this patient did not have any of these findings, it is an unlikely diagnosis. Option C- Truncus arteriosus: Truncus arteriosus is a condition that occurs due to failure of aorticopulmonary septal development, and a single arterial trunk that arises from the heart supplies systemic and pulmonary circulations. Initial neonatal period findings are cyanosis and murmur. Over the next few months, torrential pulmonary blood flow develops, and heart failure becomes prominent. Single and loud second heart sound is present. As this patient did not have any of these findings, it is an unlikely diagnosis. Option D- Congenital mitral stenosis: Congenital mitral stenosis can occur as an isolated finding or with coarctation of the aorta and aortic stenosis in Shone complex. Dyspnea and failure to thrive occur within the first 2 years in moderate to severe stenosis cases. The left atrium and right ventricle dilate and atrophies leading to cardiomegaly. The second heart sound is loud and split, and an apical rumbling diastolic murmur is an auscultatory finding. As this patient did not have any of these findings, it is an unlikely diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 53-year-old male presents to the medical outpatient department complaining of left-sided flank pain for the last two days. He describes intermittent dragging pain. He also reports a cough and generalized body aches. He smokes 3 to 4 cigarettes per day. He is afebrile and has a blood pressure of 160/100mmHg and a pulse rate of 81 beats per minute. His examination reveals a palpable left-sided kidney mass. His urine analysis indicates hematuria, and his X-ray cheat shows a canon ball appearance. What would be the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.stemHtml: A 53-year-old male presents to the medical outpatient department complaining of left-sided flank pain for the last two days. He describes intermittent dragging pain. He also reports a cough and generalized body aches. He smokes 3 to 4 cigarettes per day. He is afebrile and has a blood pressure of 160/100mmHg and a pulse rate of 81 beats per minute. His examination reveals a palpable left-sided kidney mass. His urine analysis indicates hematuria, and his X-ray cheat shows a canon ball appearance. What would be the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Grawitz tumor In the case mentioned above, the patient is 53 years of age and has complaints of left-sided flank pain associated with hematuria and canon ball appearance on chest X-ray. This is suggestive of renal cell carcinoma, also called Grawitz's tumor. Renal cell carcinoma is known as Grawtiz tumor or hypernephroma. It is the most common tumor of the kidney. It accounts for 85% of kidney tumors and arises from proximal convoluted tubules. Risk factors may include: Smoking Renal failure Asbestos Exposure Cadmium Hemodialysis Clinical features include: Haematuria Flank pain Palpable kidney mass Investigations include urine examination, ultrasound abdomen, CT scan abdomen, MRI and CT chest. It spreads by direct extension, lungs (canon ball appearance), hilar and paraaortic lymph nodes. Disease is managed depending on the stage. Incorrect options: Option A: Pyonephorosis Pyonephrosis is characterized by collecting system obstruction leading to infected purulent urine. There is suppurative destruction of the renal parenchyma. No canon ball appears in the lungs mentioned in the case above. Option B: Wilms tumour Wilms tumour is a pediatric tumour. In the case mentioned, the patient is 53, the least likely age for Wilms tumour. Wilms tumour occurs before the age of 5 years. It is unilateral in 95% of the cases and is caused by the deletion of the WT-1 tumour suppressor gene and WT2 located on chromosome II. Components of Wilms tumor (pneumonic : BEST) B – Blastema E – Epithelium ST – STroma Presents as TRIAD Intra-abdominal mass (Most common presentation) Fever (disappears after tumor resection) Hematuria (Gross/Microscopic) Option D: Renal carbuncle The formation of pus in the renal cortex characterizes renal carbuncle. Features may include fever and flank pain. There is pyuria but not haematuria, so there is a less likely chance of renal carbuncle in the case discussed above. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 71-year-old male with a history of intermediate risk adenocarcinoma of the prostate, Gleason 4+3=7 disease in 7/12 cores, pre-biopsy PSA 7.11 ng/ml, and was T1c N0 M0 post radiation therapy and a short course of androgen deprivation therapy, 3 years ago, and now with a stable PSA, visits you and is worried that his sons will develop the disease as well. He asks you about prostate cancer prevention. Which of the following statements about chemoprevention for prostate cancer is true?
questions.stemHtml: A 71-year-old male with a history of intermediate risk adenocarcinoma of the prostate, Gleason 4+3=7 disease in 7/12 cores, pre-biopsy PSA 7.11 ng/ml, and was T1c N0 M0 post radiation therapy and a short course of androgen deprivation therapy, 3 years ago, and now with a stable PSA, visits you and is worried that his sons will develop the disease as well. He asks you about prostate cancer prevention. Which of the following statements about chemoprevention for prostate cancer is true?

options.label: A
options.text: A number of randomized trials have failed to demonstrate a reduction in prostate cancer with any chemopreventive agent.

options.label: B
options.text: A randomized trial of supplementation with Vitamin E and Selenium demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer.

options.label: C
options.text: A randomized trial of supplementation with finasteride demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer.

options.label: D
options.text: A randomized trial of supplementation with boron demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer.

questions.answerText: A randomized trial of supplementation with finasteride demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer.
questions.solution: Correct Option C - A randomized trial of supplementation with finasteride demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer Randomized, placebo-controlled studies of finasteride and duterastide (both 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors) have demonstrated a significant decrease in the incidence of prostate cancer. Additionally, a randomized trial studying supplementation with Vitamin E and selenium demonstrated NO benefit. The Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial randomized 18,882 men 55 years of age or older with a normal digital rectal examination (DRE) and a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level ≤ 3.0 ng/ml to treatment with finasteride (5 mg per day) or placebo for seven years. A prostate biopsy was recommended if the annual PSA level, adjusted for the effect of finasteride, exceeded 4.0 ng/ml or if the DRE was abnormal. In the final analysis, prostate cancer was detected in 18.4% of the men in the finasteride group and 24.4% of the men in the placebo group (p < 0.001). Sexual side effects were more common in finasteride arm, whereas urinary symptoms were more common in the placebo arm. Incorrect Options: Option A - A number of randomized trials have failed to demonstrate a reduction in prostate cancer with any chemopreventive agent This option is incorrect because randomized trials of chemopreventive agents have actually shown some positive results in reducing the incidence of prostate cancer. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of dutasteride (0.5 mg daily) versus placebo in men 50 to 75 years of age with a PSA of 2.5 to 10.0 ng/ml with a negative prostate biopsy within 6 months of enrolment also demonstrated a benefit. Prostate cancer was detected in 19.9% patients in the dutasteride group vs. 25.1% in the placebo group (p < 0.001). Taken together, the two studies demonstrate a significant decrease in prostate cancer with the use of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors. Option B - A randomized trial of supplementation with Vitamin E and Selenium demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer The SELECT Trial was a randomized placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of 35,533 men 55 years or older with a PSA ≤ 4.0 ng/ml and normal DRE who were randomized one of four groups (selenium, vitamin E, selenium + vitamin E, and placebo). With a median follow-up of 5.46 years, there were no significant differences (p > 0.15 in all) in any other pre-specified cancer end points between the arms. The authors concluded that selenium or vitamin E, alone or in combination, did not prevent prostate cancer in a population of relatively healthy men. Option D - A randomized trial of supplementation with boron demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer No randomized trial has demonstrated that supplementation with boron reduces the incidence of prostate cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option C - A randomized trial of supplementation with finasteride demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer

  • Randomized, placebo-controlled studies of finasteride and duterastide (both 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors) have demonstrated a significant decrease in the incidence of prostate cancer. Additionally, a randomized trial studying supplementation with Vitamin E and selenium demonstrated NO benefit.
  • The Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial randomized 18,882 men 55 years of age or older with a normal digital rectal examination (DRE) and a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level ≤ 3.0 ng/ml to treatment with finasteride (5 mg per day) or placebo for seven years. A prostate biopsy was recommended if the annual PSA level, adjusted for the effect of finasteride, exceeded 4.0 ng/ml or if the DRE was abnormal. In the final analysis, prostate cancer was detected in 18.4% of the men in the finasteride group and 24.4% of the men in the placebo group (p < 0.001). Sexual side effects were more common in finasteride arm, whereas urinary symptoms were more common in the placebo arm.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - A number of randomized trials have failed to demonstrate a reduction in prostate cancer with any chemopreventive agent

  • This option is incorrect because randomized trials of chemopreventive agents have actually shown some positive results in reducing the incidence of prostate cancer. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of dutasteride (0.5 mg daily) versus placebo in men 50 to 75 years of age with a PSA of 2.5 to 10.0 ng/ml with a negative prostate biopsy within 6 months of enrolment also demonstrated a benefit. Prostate cancer was detected in 19.9% patients in the dutasteride group vs. 25.1% in the placebo group (p < 0.001). Taken together, the two studies demonstrate a significant decrease in prostate cancer with the use of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors.

Option B - A randomized trial of supplementation with Vitamin E and Selenium demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer

  • The SELECT Trial was a randomized placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of 35,533 men 55 years or older with a PSA ≤ 4.0 ng/ml and normal DRE who were randomized one of four groups (selenium, vitamin E, selenium + vitamin E, and placebo). With a median follow-up of 5.46 years, there were no significant differences (p > 0.15 in all) in any other pre-specified cancer end points between the arms. The authors concluded that selenium or vitamin E, alone or in combination, did not prevent prostate cancer in a population of relatively healthy men.

Option D - A randomized trial of supplementation with boron demonstrated a reduction in prostate cancer

  • No randomized trial has demonstrated that supplementation with boron reduces the incidence of prostate cancer.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old female is being treated for breast cancer with chemo-radiotherapy. During her treatment, she starts complaining of excessive urination and thirst. A complete physical exam and a thorough biochemical evaluation are done. A diagnosis of central diabetes insipidus (CDI) is made. An MRI is done and shows a space-occupying lesion in the pituitary gland. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 59-year-old female is being treated for breast cancer with chemo-radiotherapy. During her treatment, she starts complaining of excessive urination and thirst. A complete physical exam and a thorough biochemical evaluation are done. A diagnosis of central diabetes insipidus (CDI) is made. An MRI is done and shows a space-occupying lesion in the pituitary gland. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Metastasis to the pituitary: This patient has been diagnosed with CDI, and it is necessary to rule out a space-occupying lesion as a cause. It is important to know that in patients with a pituitary adenoma, about 1% are associated with CDI. Most often, pituitary adenomas affect the anterior rather than the posterior pituitary cells. CDI is more likely to be caused by metastasis to the pituitary gland. Plus, patients with breast cancer are 9.3 times more likely to develop metastasis to the pituitary gland. The most common source of pituitary metastases is breast cancer. Incorrect Options: Option A- Pituitary adenoma: Pituitary adenomas are less likely to cause CDI compared to metastases. Option B- Craniopharyngioma: Craniopharyngiomas are more likely to be seen in younger patients. A patient with breast cancer is statistically more likely to develop pituitary metastases than a craniopharyngioma. They are also more likely to cause anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. Only about 15% of patients with a craniopharyngioma develop CDI. Option D- Combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy tend to target rapidly dividing cells. Since cells of the central nervous system are not rapidly dividing, they are unlikely to be affected. It is exceedingly rare for radiotherapy to induce necrosis or inflammation of the pituitary gland. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with frequent episodes of weakness and fatigue over the past several months. She has also noticed increased urinary frequency and thirst. There is no history of nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. She denies any recent travel, sick contacts, or exposure to toxins. Physical Examination her blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg; heart rate is 80 beats per minute. Her respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute and her oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Laboratory investigations reveal serum sodium: 138 mmol/L, serum potassium: 2.9 mmol/L, serum chloride: 95 mmol/L, serum bicarbonate: 28 mmol/L, and serum creatinine: 0.8 mg/dL. Urine analysis shows urine sodium: 25 mmol/L, urine potassium: 60 mmol/L, urine chloride: 50 mmol/L, and urine calcium: 2.5 mmol/L. Renal ultrasound and a 24-hour urine collection for electrolytes were both normal. The patient was diagnosed with Type 3 Bartter Syndrome. What is the pathophysiology of this Syndrome?

options.label: A
options.text: Impaired reabsorption of sodium in the ascending loop of Henle

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Impaired reabsorption of sodium in the ascending loop of Henle
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Impaired reabsorption of sodium in the ascending loop of Henle: Type 3 Bartter Syndrome is a rare genetic disorder caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the ascending loop of Henle. The impaired function of this cotransporter leads to increased urinary losses of sodium, potassium, and calcium, as well as hypomagnesemia. It leads to electrolyte imbalances, including hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Clinical features: It typically presents in infancy or early childhood with symptoms such as failure to thrive, polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, and constipation. Patients may also experience muscle weakness, cramps, and tetany due to hypokalemia. Nephrocalcinosis (calcium deposition in the kidney) may also occur in some patients. Lab investigations: Hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and increased sodium, potassium, and calcium excretion in the urine is seen. Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis of Type 3 Bartter Syndrome by identifying mutations in the CLCNKB gene encoding the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter. Imaging studies, such as ultrasound or CT scans, may show signs of nephrocalcinosis. Treatment options: It focuses on correcting the electrolyte imbalances and managing symptoms. It may include potassium and magnesium supplementation, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to reduce calcium excretion and prevent nephrocalcinosis. Incorrect Options: Option B- Decreased secretion of aldosterone by the adrenal gland: Aldosterone secretion is not affected in this condition. It is caused by conditions such as Addison's disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or adrenal gland tumors or lesions that impair aldosterone production. Decreased aldosterone secretion leads to electrolyte imbalances, including hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. Clinical features include weakness, fatigue, dehydration, and low blood pressure. Lab findings include hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis. Treatment involves hormone replacement therapy to correct hormonal imbalances. Option C- Decreased reabsorption of bicarbonate in the proximal tubule: It is seen in renal tubular acidosis (RTA), a group of disorders that affect the kidney's ability to regulate acid-base balance. Many causes, including autoimmune diseases, medicines, and genetic disorders, can lead to RTA. Impaired reabsorption of bicarbonate in the proximal tubule leads to metabolic acidosis. Clinical features include weakness, fatigue, dehydration, and low blood pressure. Laboratory Investigations: include metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap, hypokalemia, and increased urinary excretion of bicarbonate. Imaging findings may be normal. Treatment involves correcting metabolic acidosis with alkali therapy and managing underlying causes if present. Option D- Impaired function of the distal convoluted tubule in the kidney: It can be seen in Gitelman Syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that affects the kidney's ability to reabsorb sodium, potassium, and chloride. Impaired reabsorption of sodium, potassium, and chloride in the distal convoluted tubule leads to electrolyte imbalances, including hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Clinical features include fatigue, muscle weakness, cramps, tetany, and occasional episodes of nausea and vomiting. Lab findings include hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and hypercalciuria. Genetic testing can identify mutations in the gene encoding the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride co-transporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Imaging findings are usually normal. Treatment involves correcting the electrolyte imbalances and managing symptoms with potassium and magnesium supplementation and a high-salt diet. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lymphoma: Lymphoma affects approximately 5% of Sjogren’s patients. The relative risk of lymphoma among Sjogren’s syndrome patients is estimated between 16 and 20. Factors that increase the risk of lymphoma in Sjogren’s syndrome include previous parotid irradiation, leg ulcers, persistent purpura, persistent enlargement of salivary glands, persistent lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Most cases are extranodal, with the commonest site being salivary glands. Other areas prone to lymphoma in Sjogren’s syndrome include the nasopharynx, thyroid, stomach and lung. MRI is the modality of choice for imaging an abnormal salivary gland, and biopsy of the affected gland is recommended to obtain definitive histology. Histologically, most are marginal zone lymphomas, such as mucosal-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma and nodal low-grade monocytoid lymphoma. Other forms of Sjogren’s associated lymphoma include diffuse large B cell lymphoma. Incorrect Options: Option A - Infectious mononucleosis: Infectious mononucleosis is unlikely given the negative monospot test. Option C - Mumps: Mumps were ruled out by unilateral parotid gland involvement. questions.solution: Correct Option C- Chronic alcohol abuse: A known risk factor for the onset of myocarditis is chronic alcohol usage. Alcohol can have toxic effects on the heart muscle, which can result in inflammation and cell damage. Chronic alcohol misuse can also impair immunity, leaving the body more vulnerable to illnesses resulting in myocarditis. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypertension: A chronic illness known as hypertension causes higher arterial blood pressure. Although many cardiovascular disorders, such as coronary artery disease and heart failure, are at increased risk due to hypertension, myocarditis is not one of them. Option B- Hyperlipidemia: Although hyperlipidemia is not a known risk factor for myocarditis, it is a risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Option D- Diabetes Mellitus: A chronic metabolic condition called diabetes mellitus is characterized by elevated blood sugar levels. Diabetes is an established risk factor for coronary artery disease and heart failure, among other cardiovascular disorders, but it is not one for myocarditis. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following tests should you order next to determine the most likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Serum cryoglobulins: Chronic HCV infection is strongly associated with glomerular disease. The primary types of glomerular disease associated with HCV infection include mixed cryoglobulinemia syndrome, membranous nephropathy, and polyarteritis nodosa. Mixed cryoglobulinemia, a systemic vasculitis, results in symptoms that include fevers, purpura, arthralgia, renal disease, and neuropathy. Hematuria, proteinuria, and renal impairment may be seen. Laboratory studies reveals circulating cryoglobulins and hypocomplementemia. Clinical findings are the result of precipitation and deposition of cold-insoluble HCV-containing immune complexes in the kidneys, peripheral nerves, and skin. Incorrect Options: Option A - Anti-smooth muscle antibody: This is a non-specific test and will not make the diagnosis. Option B - Skin biopsy of the lesion: Although skin biopsy may reveal leukocytoclastic vasculitis or occasionally cryoglobulin within the lumen of vessels in the skin, the initial test is an assay of serum cryoglobulins. Option C - Renal biopsy: Renal biopsy is not the first diagnostic test recommended for this patient. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male comes to the emergency department due to acute left leg pain for the past 30 minutes. He says that he was at home watching TV when the pain occurred suddenly and severely. His medical history is significant for hypertension, however, he is not compliant with his prescribed medicines. Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, a pale leg, an absent left popliteal pulse, and decreased sensation to pin prick. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male comes to the emergency department due to acute left leg pain for the past 30 minutes. He says that he was at home watching TV when the pain occurred suddenly and severely. His medical history is significant for hypertension, however, he is not compliant with his prescribed medicines. Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular pulse, a pale leg, an absent left popliteal pulse, and decreased sensation to pin prick. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Atrial fibrillation: This patient’s presentation with acute leg pain, pulselessness, pallor, and paresthesia is suggestive of acute limb ischemia secondary to thromboembolism. An irregularly irregular pulse along with a presentation of acute limb ischemia is consistent with atrial fibrillation Pathogenesis of A-fib is characterized by abnormal automatic firing and the presence of multiple interacting reentry circuits looping around the atria . Episodes of AF are initiated by rapid bursts of ectopic beats arising from conducting tissue in the pulmonary veins or from diseased/dilated atrial tissue. Atrial fibrillation most commonly occurs due to atrial remodeling as a result of hypertension (as in this patient) and other cardiac disorders e.g. mitral stenosis. Atrial fibrillation results in stasis of blood flow in the left atrium . As a result, there is an increased risk of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage. This thrombus can subsequently embolize into the systemic circulation and lead to ischemia of the affected region. Incorrect Options: Option B- Atherosclerosis: Atherosclerosis is a chronic process characterized by the accumulation of cholesterol plaques in the arteries which leads to a reduction in blood flow. It can lead to chronic limb ischemia rather than acute limb ischemia. Chronic limb ischemia presents with limb claudication and diminished pulses. Option C- Compartment syndrome: Compartment syndrome is characterized by increased pressure within a muscle compartment , leading to decreased blood flow and subsequent damage to nerves and muscles It most commonly occurs as a result of traumatic limb fractures This patient with an irregular pulse and no history of trauma is most likely suffering from A-fib Option D- Deep Vein Thrombosis: DVT presents with pain and swelling of the leg rather than pulselessness and pallor. It usually occurs in a hypercoagulable state e.g. pregnancy and reduced mobility e.g. after surgery This patient with an irregular pulse and acute limb ischemia is most likely suffering from A-fib @Neet_pg_bot

  • It can lead to chronic limb ischemia rather than acute limb ischemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following enteric infections is closely associated with PPI treatment in the absence of antibiotic use?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following enteric infections is closely associated with PPI treatment in the absence of antibiotic use?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Clostridioides difficile: Difficile is the enteric pathogen most closely associated with PPI use. A reduction in gastric acid secretion is associated with an increased risk of infection and will also allow pathogenic organisms to colonize the upper GI tract, which may increase the risk of pneumonia. C. difficile is an anaerobic spore-forming bacterium, and acid-resistant spores are implicated as a factor causing an increased risk of C. difficile infection. Antisecretory therapy with PPIs is associated with recurrent and new C. difficile infection and with higher rates of infection than with H2 receptor antagonists. Patients with persistent diarrhea who are treated with PPI inhibitors should undergo testing for C. difficile, and the FDA recommends the use of PPI therapy at the lowest possible dose for the shortest duration needed. Incorrect Options: Option A - Salmonella: Salmonella infection has been reported in association with PPI use, but the strength of this association is unclear. Option B - Enterobacter: Shigella is a major cause of bacterial diarrhea but has not been associated with PPI use. Option D - Campylobacter: Although Campylobacter infections have been associated with PPI use, the risk is not clear. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman has been referred to your pulmonology OPD for evaluation of right-sided pleuritic chest pain. The patient does not smoke and has no occupational exposures, but during her early twenties her husband worked in a ship-yard with probable asbestos exposure. What is the earliest detectable physiologic abnormality expected in this patient as a result of asbestos exposure?

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced vital capacity with preserved FEV1

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Decreased DLCO and pulmonary compliance: Asbestosis is a restrictive lung disease. This patient was exposed to asbestos as a result of living in close proximity to an asbestos worker, with secondary exposure. The earliest physiologic abnormalities detectable in asbestos-exposed patients is a decrease in DLCO (Diffusion Capacity of Lung for Carbon Monoxide) and diminished pulmonary compliance. Carbon monoxide uptake is a function of both membrane conductance (which represents diffusion across the alveolar-capillary interface, and reactive conductance) the chemical reaction between CO and hemoglobin. In asbestosis, pulmonary fibrosis, and emphysema, the membrane surface area is reduced, reducing conductance across the alveolar-capillary interface and subsequently reducing DLCO. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hypoxemia at rest: Hypoxemia at rest usually indicates advanced lung disease. In the early stages of asbestosis, patients typically exhibit normal oxygen levels at rest, though they may experience exertional hypoxemia. Option C - Reduced vital capacity with preserved FEV1: Reduced vital capacity indicates restrictive lung disease. However, in asbestosis, this typically only becomes evident later in the disease process, once significant fibrotic changes have occurred. Thus, this is not the earliest detectable physiologic abnormality. Option D - Reduced FEV1/FVC ratio: Asbestosis, being a restrictive lung disease, typically presents with a normal or even increased FEV1/FVC ratio. This is due to a proportional reduction in both FEV1 and FVC. In contrast, obstructive lung diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or asthma, present with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio due to the disproportionate reduction in FEV1. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of following is the mechanism of action associated with short-chain fatty acid therapy in the treatment of chronic radiation proctitis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of following is the mechanism of action associated with short-chain fatty acid therapy in the treatment of chronic radiation proctitis?

options.label: A
options.text: Stimulates mucosa blood flow and regeneration

options.label: B
options.text: Acts as a chemical sclerosant of the blood vessels

options.label: D
options.text: Prevents release of destructive hydrolases from inflammatory cells

questions.answerText: Stimulates mucosa blood flow and regeneration
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Stimulates mucosa blood flow and regeneration: Short-chain fatty acid therapy may help heal chronic changes associated with radiation therapy by promoting the development of new blood vessels and healing of the damaged rectal mucosa. In contrast, formalin serves as a sclerosant of the blood vessels in the area and prevents flares of proctitis by reducing the release of inflammatory cells and mediators in the rectum. Topical sulfasalazine inhibits the production of inflammatory cytokines, while topical steroids prevent the release of destructive hydrolases from inflammatory cells. Topical sucralfate has a favorable effect on epithelial microvascular injury. A small trial showed the clinical response for sucralfate enemas was better compared with oral sulfasalazine and prednisolone enemas, although no endoscopic difference was noted. In patients with persistent or severe bleeding due to chronic radiation proctitis, guidelines suggest an initial trial of sucralfate enemas. In patients with persistent or severe bleeding due to chronic radiation proctitis and in patients with tenesmus or rectal pain, an initial trial of sucralfate enemas is recommended. Incorrect Options: Option B - Acts as a chemical sclerosant of the blood vessels: This is not the mechanism of action associated with short-chain fatty acid therapy in the treatment of chronic radiation proctitis. Sclerosants are substances that cause the blood vessels to become fibrotic and close off. In the context of chronic radiation proctitis, promoting blood vessel closure would not be beneficial as it can exacerbate tissue damage and inflammation. Option C - Inhibits production of inflammatory cytokines: This is not the mechanism of action of short-chain fatty acid therapy in chronic radiation proctitis. While short-chain fatty acids may have some anti-inflammatory effects, their primary mode of action in this condition is related to mucosal blood flow and regeneration. Option D - Prevents the release of destructive hydrolases from inflammatory cells: This is also not the mechanism of action associated with short-chain fatty acid therapy in the treatment of chronic radiation proctitis. Short-chain fatty acids do not directly prevent the release of destructive hydrolases from inflammatory cells. Instead, they work on improving the health and regeneration of the mucosal lining, which indirectly helps mitigate inflammation and tissue damage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy comes to the clinic with hematuria, hearing loss, and anterior lens bulging. His family history reveals a pattern of renal disease affecting multiple generations. Which genetic mutation causes this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy comes to the clinic with hematuria, hearing loss, and anterior lens bulging. His family history reveals a pattern of renal disease affecting multiple generations. Which genetic mutation causes this condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- COL4A5 gene: Alport syndrome is a genetic disorder affecting the glomerular basement membrane . The most common form is X-linked Alport syndrome , caused by mutations in the COL4A5 gene encoding the α5 chain of type IV collagen . Type IV collagen is a major component of the glomerular basement membrane, and its defective formation due to COL4A5 mutations results in structural abnormalities, leading to hematuria and progressive renal disease . Kidney biopsy findings in Alport syndrome reveal irregular thickening and thinning of the glomerular basement membrane with a characteristic basket-weave appearance on electron microscopy. Hearing loss in Alport syndrome is sensorineural . Eye abnormalities may include anterior lenticonus (lens bulging), posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy, and retinal thinning. Management of Alport syndrome includes: Monitoring kidney function Hypertension control Kidney transplant is the definitive treatment Incorrect Options: Option B- SLC12A3 gene: Mutations in the SLC12A3 gene cause Gitelman syndrome . It is caused by a defect in the sodium-chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Laboratory investigations reveal: Hypokalemia Hypomagnesemia Hypocalciuria Metabolic alkalosis Gitelman syndrome does not typically present with hearing loss or ocular abnormalities. Option C- PKD1 gene: PKD1 gene mutations are responsible for causing autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). ADPKD usually presents in adulthood and is characterised by bilaterally enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts , hypertension, hematuria, and lower back pain. ADPKD does not typically present with hearing loss or ocular abnormalities. Option D- CLCN5 gene: CLCN5 gene mutation causes Dent disease , an X-linked recessive disorder. Clinical features of Dent disease include: Proteinuria, Hypercalciuria Nephrocalcinosis Kidney stones Dent disease does not typically present with hearing loss or ocular abnormalities. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the serologic evaluation of intrahepatic biliary lesions is true?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements regarding the serologic evaluation of intrahepatic biliary lesions is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Hepatic function testing is less severely abnormal with intrahepatic lesions than it is with extrahepatic biliary lesions

options.label: B
options.text: Bilirubin is more likely to be elevated with intrahepatic lesions than with extrahepatic lesions

options.label: C
options.text: Alkaline phosphatase can be used to distinguish between malignant and benign biliary strictures

options.label: D
options.text: A negative CA-19-9 level will exclude the possibility of a stricture being malignant

questions.answerText: Hepatic function testing is less severely abnormal with intrahepatic lesions than it is with extrahepatic biliary lesions
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hepatic function testing is less severely abnormal with intrahepatic lesions than it is with extrahepatic biliary lesions: Studies have shown that intrahepatic biliary lesions will have abnormally elevated liver function tests about 65% of the time, namely alkaline phosphatase and GGT. However, bilirubin is almost never elevated with intrahepatic lesions. The ability of elevations in alkaline phosphatase to differentiate between malignant and benign intrahepatic biliary strictures is unclear. Some studies have shown that alkaline phosphatase levels of 200 IU/L or more can help distinguish between malignant and benign strictures, while others have not. Thus, while it may help support a diagnosis of a malignant or benign stricture, it is not a diagnostic test. The same can be said for CA-19-9. Incorrect Options: Option B - Bilirubin is more likely to be elevated with intrahepatic lesions than with extrahepatic lesions: This statement is not true. In general, extrahepatic biliary obstruction is more likely to lead to elevated bilirubin levels due to the obstruction of bile flow from the liver to the intestines. Option C - Alkaline phosphatase can be used to distinguish between malignant and benign biliary strictures: Alkaline phosphatase levels can be elevated in both malignant and benign biliary strictures. While it can provide information about biliary obstruction, it alone cannot reliably distinguish between malignancy and benignity. Option D - A negative CA-19-9 level will exclude the possibility of a stricture being malignant: CA-19-9 is a tumor marker that can be elevated in cases of pancreatic and biliary tract cancers, but its absence does not definitively rule out malignancy. Other factors and tests are necessary to evaluate the nature of a stricture. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease. There is a higher risk of disease progression with increased proteinuria. Which drug is best to reduce disease progression due to proteinuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman was diagnosed with chronic kidney disease. There is a higher risk of disease progression with increased proteinuria. Which drug is best to reduce disease progression due to proteinuria?

options.label: B
options.text: Combination therapy with ACE and ARB

questions.solution: Correct Option C- ACE inhibitors or ARB: Angiotensin receptor blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors decrease proteinuria hence the CKD progression rate. ACE inhibitors or ARB reduce proteinuria by reducing glomerular perfusion pressure and benefit patients with proteinuria (ACR>30mg/mmol or PCR>50mg/mmol). There will be an immediate reduction in GFR after starting ACE inhibitors or ARB. GFR should be measured 7-10 days after the drug initiation or increasing dose. Treatment should be stopped if there is a reduction in GFR greater than 25% and still declining. Patients with hyperkalemia (>5.5mmol/L) should not be prescribed ACE inhibitors or ARB as they increase potassium levels. If a patient receiving ACE inhibitors or ARB develops hyperkalemia(>6mmol/L), the drug should be immediately stopped. Incorrect Options: Option A- Combination of ACE and Aliskiren: ACE inhibitors are effective in reducing proteinuria in patients with CKD. They should be started in patients with diabetic nephropathy, irrespective of hypertension. A combination of ACE inhibitors with aliskiren( renin inhibitor) should be avoided to reduce disease progression in patients with CKD, as it is associated with a higher rate of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. Option B- Combination therapy with ACE and ARB: ACE inhibitors and ARB are effective in reducing proteinuria in patients with CKD. They should be started in patients with CKD and proteinuria, regardless of whether the patient is hypertensive. A combination of ACE inhibitors with ARB should be avoided to reduce disease progression in patients with CKD, as it is associated with a higher rate of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. Option D- Thiazide diuretics: The drug of choice in patients with CKD and proteinuria is ACE inhibitor or ARB. Thiazide diuretics decrease proteinuria by>35% and are more effective with a low-salt diet. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C- ACE inhibitors or ARB:

  • Angiotensin receptor blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors decrease proteinuria hence the CKD progression rate.
  • ACE inhibitors or ARB reduce proteinuria by reducing glomerular perfusion pressure and benefit patients with proteinuria (ACR>30mg/mmol or PCR>50mg/mmol).
  • There will be an immediate reduction in GFR after starting ACE inhibitors or ARB.
  • GFR should be measured 7-10 days after the drug initiation or increasing dose.
  • Treatment should be stopped if there is a reduction in GFR greater than 25% and still declining.
  • Patients with hyperkalemia (>5.5mmol/L) should not be prescribed ACE inhibitors or ARB as they increase potassium levels. If a patient receiving ACE inhibitors or ARB develops hyperkalemia(>6mmol/L), the drug should be immediately stopped.

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Combination of ACE and Aliskiren:

  • ACE inhibitors are effective in reducing proteinuria in patients with CKD. They should be started in patients with diabetic nephropathy, irrespective of hypertension.
  • A combination of ACE inhibitors with aliskiren( renin inhibitor) should be avoided to reduce disease progression in patients with CKD, as it is associated with a higher rate of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury.

Option B- Combination therapy with ACE and ARB:

  • ACE inhibitors and ARB are effective in reducing proteinuria in patients with CKD. They should be started in patients with CKD and proteinuria, regardless of whether the patient is hypertensive.
  • A combination of ACE inhibitors with ARB should be avoided to reduce disease progression in patients with CKD, as it is associated with a higher rate of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury.

Option D- Thiazide diuretics:

  • The drug of choice in patients with CKD and proteinuria is ACE inhibitor or ARB.
  • Thiazide diuretics decrease proteinuria by>35% and are more effective with a low-salt diet.

questions.stem: After undergoing resection for a pheochromocytoma, a 41 year old gentleman has recurrence with several liver metastases. What therapy would you recommend?
questions.stemHtml: After undergoing resection for a pheochromocytoma, a 41 year old gentleman has recurrence with several liver metastases. What therapy would you recommend?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Iobenguane-Iodine-131 This is a radiotherapeutic drug specifically designed to treat metastatic or recurrent pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, tumors that are rare and originate from cells in the adrenal glands. Iobenguane I-131, also known as MIBG I-131 or by the trade name Azedra, is taken up by adrenergic tissue (including these types of tumors) and emits radiation, leading to cell death. Incorrect Options: Option B - CVD: This is a combination of cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and dacarbazine. It's a chemotherapy regimen used in the treatment of various cancers, including some neuroendocrine tumors like pheochromocytoma. However, it's generally used when other treatments aren't possible or have failed, and it can have significant side effects. Iobenguane I-131 is generally preferred for metastatic or recurrent pheochromocytoma due to its specificity for adrenergic tissue. Option C - Temozolomide: This is an oral chemotherapy drug that's primarily used to treat certain types of brain tumors, like glioblastoma multiforme and anaplastic astrocytoma. It's not typically used in the treatment of pheochromocytoma. Option D - FOLFOX: This is a combination of folinic acid (leucovorin), fluorouracil (5-FU), and oxaliplatin. It's a chemotherapy regimen that's primarily used to treat colorectal cancer. It's not typically used in the treatment of pheochromocytoma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is true of gastric acid secretion?

options.label: A
options.text: Gastric acid is secreted primarily by parietal cells as well as by G cells.

options.label: B
options.text: The parietal cells secrete pure hydrochloric acid at a concentration equivalent to a pH of 0.8.

options.label: C
options.text: Parietal cells have membrane receptors for 4 stimulants.

options.label: D
options.text: The only inhibitory receptors on the parietal cell are somatostatin receptors.

questions.answerText: The parietal cells secrete pure hydrochloric acid at a concentration equivalent to a pH of 0.8.
questions.solution: Correct Option B - The parietal cells secrete pure hydrochloric acid at a concentration equivalent to a pH of 0.8: Gastric juice is made up of both parietal and non parietal secretions, with parietal cell secretion of pure hydrochloric acid at a concentration equivalent to pH of 0.8. Non Parietal secretions include mucus, electrolytes, and water. Incorrect Options: Option A - Gastric acid is secreted primarily by parietal cells as well as by G cells: G cells release gastrin, which acts on the cholecystokinin receptor of the parietal cell. Option C - Parietal cells have membrane receptors for 4 stimulants: Parietal cells have basolateral membrane receptors for histamine (H2-receptor), acetylcholine (muscarinic M3 cholinergic receptor), and cholecystokinin (CCKB). These are the only receptors for stimulation. Option D - The only inhibitory receptors on the parietal cell are somatostatin receptors: Parietal cells have receptors on the basolateral membrane for inhibitors, including somatostatin and prostaglandins. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with chest pain that radiates to his left arm. He reports that the pain began about an hour ago while he was mowing the lawn. His past medical history is significant for hypertension. On examination, he appears uncomfortable, his blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and he has a regular rhythm. A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which of the following events occurs during ventricular systole?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with chest pain that radiates to his left arm. He reports that the pain began about an hour ago while he was mowing the lawn. His past medical history is significant for hypertension. On examination, he appears uncomfortable, his blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and he has a regular rhythm. A 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which of the following events occurs during ventricular systole?
questions.solution: Option C: Ventricular ejection Ventricular ejection occurs during ventricular systole , which is the phase of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles contract to pump blood into the systemic circulation. During ventricular ejection, the pressure in the ventricles exceeds the pressure in the aorta , causing the aortic valve to open and blood to be ejected into the aorta. The left ventricle ejects blood first , followed by the right ventricle. Option A: Ventricular filling Ventricular filling occurs during ventricular diastole , which is the phase of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles relax and fill with blood from the atria. Option B: Isovolumetric contraction Isovolumetric contraction occurs during early ventricular systole when the ventricles contract and increase in pressure, but the aortic and pulmonary valves are still closed, so no blood is being ejected yet. Option D: Isovolumetric relaxatio n It occurs during early ventricular diastole when the ventricles relax and decrease in pressure , but the aortic and pulmonary valves are still closed, so no blood is flowing into or out of the ventricles. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Option C: Ventricular ejection

  • Ventricular ejection occurs during ventricular systole, which is the phase of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles contract to pump blood into the systemic circulation.
  • During ventricular ejection, the pressure in the ventricles exceeds the pressure in the aorta, causing the aortic valve to open and blood to be ejected into the aorta.
  • The left ventricle ejects blood first, followed by the right ventricle.

Option A: Ventricular filling

  • Ventricular filling occurs during ventricular diastole, which is the phase of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles relax and fill with blood from the atria.

Option B: Isovolumetric contraction

  • Isovolumetric contraction occurs during early ventricular systole when the ventricles contract and increase in pressure, but the aortic and pulmonary valves are still closed, so no blood is being ejected yet.

Option D: Isovolumetric relaxation

  • It occurs during early ventricular diastole when the ventricles relax and decrease in pressure, but the aortic and pulmonary valves are still closed, so no blood is flowing into or out of the ventricles.

questions.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has been recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. He is currently managed with diet and lifestyle modification. On examination his blood pressure is 144/75 mmHg, his BMI is 33 kg/m2, his body weight is 93 kg and his waist circumference is 102 cm. He has just completed the EXPERT patient education program and his most recent HbA1c is (6.7%) ( normal is less than (6.5 %)). On review in the clinic he is well but requests some further information relating to the glycaemic index of food to the management of his diabetes. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice relating to glycaemic index for this gentleman?

options.label: A
options.text: Low glycaemic index foods are associated with slower rates of carbohydrate digestion and greater hepatic and peripheral tissue carbohydrate extraction.

options.label: B
options.text: The glycaemic index is a measure of insulin response to food ingestion

options.label: C
options.text: A baked potato is an example of a low glycaemic index food

options.label: D
options.text: Low glycaemic index foods characteristically have a low carbohydrate content.

questions.answerText: Low glycaemic index foods are associated with slower rates of carbohydrate digestion and greater hepatic and peripheral tissue carbohydrate extraction.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Low glycaemic index foods are associated with slower rates of carbohydrate digestion and greater hepatic and peripheral tissue carbohydrate extraction: The Glycaemic index or GI is a measure of the effects of carbohydrates on blood glucose levels. Carbohydrates that break down rapidly during digestion releasing glucose rapidly into the bloodstream and have a high GI; carbohydrates that break down slowly, releasing glucose gradually into the bloodstream, have a low GI. For most people, foods with a low GI have significant health benefits. The concept was developed by Dr. David J. Jenkins and colleagues in 1980–1981. A lower glycaemic index suggests slower rates of digestion and absorption of the foods' carbohydrates and may also indicate greater extraction from the liver and periphery of the products of carbohydrate digestion. A lower glycaemic response is often thought to equate to a lower insulin demand, better long-term blood glucose control and a reduction in blood lipids. The insulin index may therefore also be useful as it provides a direct measure of the insulin response to a food. The glycaemic index of a food is defined as the area under the two hour blood glucose response curve (AUC) following the ingestion of a fixed portion of carbohydrate (usually 50 g). The AUC of the test food is divided by the AUC of the standard (either glucose or white bread, giving two different definitions) and multiplied by 100. The average GI value is calculated from data collected in 10 human subjects. Both the standard and test food must contain an equal amount of available carbohydrate. The result gives a relative ranking for each tested food. The current validated methods use glucose as the reference food, giving it a glycaemic index value of 100 by definition. This has the advantages that it is universal and it results in maximum GI values of approximately 100. White bread can also be used as a reference food, giving a different set of GI values (if white bread = 100, then glucose ≈ 140). For people whose staple carbohydrate source is white bread, this has the advantage of conveying directly whether replacement of the dietary staple with a different food would result in faster or slower blood glucose response. The disadvantages with this system are that the reference food is not well-defined, and the GI scale is culture dependent. A low GI food will release glucose more slowly and steadily. A high GI food causes a more rapid rise in blood glucose levels and is suitable for energy recovery after endurance exercise or for a person with diabetes experiencing hypoglycaemia. The glycaemic effect of foods depends on a number of factors such as the type of starch (amylose vs amylopectin), physical entrapment of the starch molecules within the food, fat and protein content of the food and organic acids or their salts in the meal — adding vinegar for example, will lower the GI. The presence of fat or soluble dietary fibre can slow the gastric emptying rate thus lowering the GI. Unrefined breads with higher amounts of fibre generally have a lower GI value than white breads. Many brown breads, however, are treated with enzymes to soften the crust, which makes the starch more accessible (high GI). While adding butter or oil will lower the GI of a meal, the GI ranking does not change. That is, with or without additions, there is still a higher blood glucose curve after white bread than after a low GI bread. The glycaemic index can only be applied to foods with reasonable carbohydrate content, as the test relies on subjects consuming enough of the test food to yield about 50 g of available carbohydrate. Many fruits and vegetables (but not potatoes) contain very little carbohydrate per serving and thus the GI is negligible. This also applies to carrots, which were originally and incorrectly reported as having a high GI. Alcoholic beverages have been reported to have low GI values, but it should be noted that beer has a moderate GI. Recent studies have shown that the consumption of an alcoholic drink prior to a meal reduces the GI of the meal by approximately 15%. Moderate alcohol consumption more than 12 hours prior to a test does not affect the GI Incorrect Options: Option B - The glycaemic index is a measure of insulin response to food ingestion: This statement is not accurate. The glycaemic index is not a direct measure of insulin response to food ingestion. While there is some correlation between the glycaemic index and insulin response (higher glycaemic index foods can lead to higher insulin levels), the primary focus of the GI is on how quickly and how much blood glucose levels rise after consuming a specific food. Option C - A baked potato is an example of a low glycaemic index food: This statement is not accurate. A baked potato is an example of a high glycaemic index food. Potatoes, especially when cooked, have a high carbohydrate content and are rapidly digested and absorbed, leading to a significant increase in blood glucose levels. Option D - Low glycaemic index foods characteristically have a low carbohydrate content: This statement is not accurate. The glycaemic index is a measure of how quickly carbohydrates in a food raise blood glucose levels, regardless of the total carbohydrate content of the food. Some low glycaemic index foods may have a high carbohydrate content, while some high glycaemic index foods may have a low carbohydrate content. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - AST level: A study testing a model to predict the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma demonstrated that in patients with non-viral cirrhosis, those whose AST was greater than 40 U/L had a risk for hepatocellular carcinoma approaching that of those with HCV or HBV cirrhosis. questions.solution: Correct tumorsOption C: Chest CT scan to look for metastasis Given the patient's history of renal cell carcinoma and current symptoms, the most likely diagnosis is metastatic disease. A chest CT scan is a type of imaging study that uses X-rays to create detailed images of the chest, which can help identify any visible lesions that may indicate metastasis. Therefore, a chest CT scan is the best next step in management. Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) recurrence is a common concern for patients who have undergone treatment for this type of cancer. RCC can recur locally (in the kidney or nearby tissues) or spread to other body parts (metastasize), such as the lungs, bones, liver, or brain. The risk of recurrence after treatment depends on several factors, including the stage and grade of original cancer, the type of treatment received, and the patient's overall health. Generally, patients with earlier-stage and lower-grade tumors have a lower risk of recurrence than those with more advanced tumors. If RCC recurrence is suspected, further diagnostic tests, such as imaging studies (CT, MRI, or PET scans) and biopsy, may be ordered to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment options for RCC recurrence depend on the location and extent of the recurrence and the patient's overall health and preferences. Patients who have undergone treatment for RCC should be closely monitored for signs of recurrence and should communicate any new symptoms or concerns to their healthcare provider. Regular follow-up visits and imaging studies may be recommended to detect and manage recurrence early. While these medications can sometimes cause hypercalcemia as a side effect, this is typically rare. In this case, given the patient's history of renal cell carcinoma and symptoms suggestive of metastatic disease, it is more likely that the elevated calcium levels are due to cancer spread rather than medication side effects. Therefore, stopping the calcium channel blocker is not the best next step in management. Option B: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing PSA testing is a blood test used to screen for prostate cancer. While prostate cancer is common in men, it is not relevant to this patient's presentation, as he has a history of renal cell carcinoma. Therefore, PSA testing is not an appropriate next step in management. Option D: PTH level measurement Hypercalcemia (elevated calcium levels in the blood) can be caused by various conditions, including cancer, hyperparathyroidism, and certain medications. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is a hormone that helps to regulate calcium levels in the body, and measuring PTH levels can help to distinguish between different types of hypercalcemia. However, in this patient's case, given his history of renal cell carcinoma and current symptoms, metastatic disease is the most likely cause of his hypercalcemia. Therefore, a chest CT scan to evaluate for the presence of metastasis is the best next step in management. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Gliclazide: Drug-induced liver disease is generally divided into hepatocellular, cholestatic or mixed. There is however considerable overlap, with some drugs causing a range of changes to the liver. Incorrect Options: Option A - Acarbose: Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that slows down the digestion of carbohydrates in the intestine, helping to lower post-meal blood sugar levels. Option D - Metformin: Metformin is a commonly prescribed medication for type 2 diabetes that improves insulin sensitivity and reduces liver glucose production. It is generally considered safe and is not typically associated with cholestasis. @Neet_pg_bot

The ECG findings of AVNRT include regular narrow QRS complexes with no clear P waves (the P waves are hidden within the QRS complexes). AVNRT is a supraventricular tachycardia caused by a reentry circuit in the AV node. Stress, alcohol, and caffeine can trigger episodes of AVNRT. Vagal maneuvers can be done to terminate the arrhythmia in this patient. If vagal maneuvers do not terminate AVNRT, IV adenosine administration is the next step Adenosine has a rapid onset of action and successfully terminates AVNRT in over 80% of cases. During IV administration, patients should be supine and undergo continuous blood pressure and electrocardiographic monitoring. Patients with asthma and reactive airway disease should not be given adenosine because of the risk of bronchospasm. questions.stem: A 50 year-old male presents to your OPD anxious when he learnt that his older brother had been diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis and he desires to be screened for the presence of this disease. Which of the following should be obtained in his screening process?
questions.stemHtml: A 50 year-old male presents to your OPD anxious when he learnt that his older brother had been diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis and he desires to be screened for the presence of this disease. Which of the following should be obtained in his screening process?

options.label: D
options.text: Presence of skin hyperpigmentation, decreased libido and Diabetes Mellitus

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Transferrin and serum ferritin levels: In screening for hereditary hemochromatosis (HH), obtaining transferrin and serum ferritin levels is essential. These tests help evaluate iron status and the likelihood of iron overload in individuals with suspected or confirmed family history of HH. Transferrin: Transferrin is a protein that binds to iron in the blood and transports it throughout the body. Transferrin saturation (TSAT) is calculated by dividing serum iron levels by total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). Elevated TSAT levels can indicate increased iron absorption. Serum Ferritin: Serum ferritin is a marker of iron stores in the body. Elevated serum ferritin levels are indicative of iron overload. It is important to note that while serum ferritin is a useful marker, it can also be elevated due to other conditions such as inflammation or liver disease. However, in the context of HH screening, elevated serum ferritin levels should raise suspicion. Incorrect Options: Option A - Haemoglobin and Transferrin Saturation Levels: While hemoglobin levels and transferrin saturation levels can provide some information about iron status, they alone are not sufficient for the comprehensive screening of hereditary hemochromatosis. Serum ferritin and genetic testing play more significant roles in diagnosis and risk assessment. Option C - Liver Biopsy: Liver biopsy is an invasive procedure that may be used to assess iron overload and damage in the liver. However, it is not typically used as a first-line screening tool for hereditary hemochromatosis. Non-invasive methods such as transferrin and serum ferritin levels, along with imaging studies, are generally preferred before considering a liver biopsy. Option D - Presence of Skin Hyperpigmentation, Decreased Libido, and Diabetes Mellitus: These clinical findings can indeed occur in advanced stages of hereditary hemochromatosis, but they are not specific enough for screening purposes. By the time these symptoms manifest, significant iron overload and organ damage may have already occurred. Therefore, relying solely on clinical symptoms for screening is not optimal, and laboratory testing is necessary for early detection and intervention. @Neet_pg_bot

MRI brain revealed a multifocal process involving only white matter, not enhancing with Gadolinium contrast, with no mass affect, and there does not appear to be a predilection for any vascular territory. Which of the following tests would be most helpful in making a correct diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: 110 days after undergoing a matched sibling donor related stem cell transplant for high-risk AML, a 47 year old female patient is brought to her transplant center by family with h/o 2 episodes of seizures the last week and bouts of visual loss and confusion during this time. MRI brain revealed a multifocal process involving only white matter, not enhancing with Gadolinium contrast, with no mass affect, and there does not appear to be a predilection for any vascular territory. Which of the following tests would be most helpful in making a correct diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Serum JC virus DNA: The clinical scenario described is highly suggestive of Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML), which is a rare and often fatal viral infection of the brain. PML is caused by the JC polyomavirus (JCV), and it primarily affects individuals with compromised immune systems, including those who have undergone stem cell transplantation. The characteristic features of PML include multifocal white matter lesions in the brain, which do not enhance with gadolinium contrast and are not confined to any specific vascular territory. To confirm the diagnosis of PML in this patient, the most helpful test would be serum JC virus DNA detection. While the gold standard for diagnosing PML is a brain biopsy, this procedure is associated with significant risks and is generally avoided due to the high morbidity and mortality associated with it. Therefore, the detection of JC virus DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) through PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is a non-invasive and accurate method for diagnosing PML. questions.solution: Correct Option C - Ophthalmoplegia, areflexia, ataxia: Miller-Fisher syndrome is a variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) that is evident in approximately 5% of cases and characterized by the triad of ophthalmoplegia, areflexia, and ataxia. It shares the features of a preceding infection, hyporeflexia, and elevated cerebrospinal fluid protein levels (without pleocytosis) with the classic form of GBS. Other features may include additional symmetric cranial nerve deficits, often as bilateral facial nerve palsies. An axonal sensory neuropathy is often detected. Unlike classic GBS, motor and demyelinating components are minimal. The disorder is associated with GQ1b and GT1a autoantibodies and may relate to a specific form of C. jejuni infection. Recovery occurs over several weeks. However, the presence of ataxia and sensory loss alone would not indicate the Miller-Fisher variant. questions.stem: A 68-year-old male was otherwise healthy until diagnosed with pancreatic carcinoma in the body of the pancreas. Today, he presents with hematemesis, and upper endoscopy reveals gastric varices. On CT, the pancreatic tumor is seen with adjacent thrombosis of the splenic vein. Which of the following is true?
questions.stemHtml: A 68-year-old male was otherwise healthy until diagnosed with pancreatic carcinoma in the body of the pancreas. Today, he presents with hematemesis, and upper endoscopy reveals gastric varices. On CT, the pancreatic tumor is seen with adjacent thrombosis of the splenic vein. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Splenectomy is the treatment of choice for most patients with splenic vein thrombosis complicated by variceal hemorrhage.

options.label: B
options.text: A wedged hepatic venous pressure gradient is likely to be normal in this patient.

options.label: C
options.text: The risk of recurrent bleeding can be reduced by diuretic and beta-blocker therapy.

questions.answerText: Splenectomy is the treatment of choice for most patients with splenic vein thrombosis complicated by variceal hemorrhage.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Splenectomy is the treatment of choice for most patients with splenic vein thrombosis complicated by variceal hemorrhage: In some studies, up to 10% of gastric varices are the result of splenic vein thrombosis, usually related to pancreatic or gastric cancer or pancreatitis. Alternatively, splenic artery embolization can be performed in patients who have extensive cancer that precludes splenectomy. Patients with gastric varices usually present with acute GI bleeding or as the result of an incidental finding on upper endoscopy. The risk of bleeding is approximately 50% over 5 years in patients who have gastric varices found incidentally. Acute bleeding can be treated in the same manner as an esophageal variceal bleed with octreotide or, if uncontrollable, with compression by Blakemore tube or gastric balloon. Incorrect Options: Option B - A wedged hepatic venous pressure gradient is likely to be normal in this patient: The wedged hepatic venous pressure gradient in patients with gastric esophageal bleeding is generally significantly more elevated in patients with gastric varices. The hepatic venous pressure gradient reflects the portal vein pressure and is accepted as the most accurate predictor of portal hypertension. In this case, the cause of the patient's portal hypertension is "prehepatic" from the splenic vein thrombosis causing disruption of the vascular system leading to increased pressure in the portal venous system, without direct involvement of the liver parenchyma. Other Prehepatic causes include splanchnic arteriovenous fistulas, and splenomegaly Option C - The risk of recurrent bleeding can be reduced by diuretic and beta-blocker therapy: The benefit of diuretic and beta-blocker therapy for the prevention of recurrent bleeding is unclear. Option D - Anticoagulation is indicated: Splenectomy or splenic artery embolization is the treatment of choice. Splenic vein thrombosis without bleeding is treated with anticoagulation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Cefepime: Cefepime is a fourth-generation cephalosporin. Fifteen percent of people with penicillin allergy have cross-reactivity to cephalosporins. When ulcers are assessed by a healthcare professional, a scoring system is used to assess how severe the ulcer is. questions.stem: A 32-year-old female is admitted to the unit for progressive shortness of breath. She was diagnosed 10 years ago with HIV infection and is being treated with HAART. Her CD4 count was 450 cells/mL 4 months ago. Which of the following factors most strongly predicts a poor prognosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old female is admitted to the unit for progressive shortness of breath. She was diagnosed 10 years ago with HIV infection and is being treated with HAART. Her CD4 count was 450 cells/mL 4 months ago. Which of the following factors most strongly predicts a poor prognosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Reason for ICU admission: HIV patients present frequently in ICU settings. An introduction of HAART therapy reduces the risk of opportunistic infections and malignant growths in this vulnerable population. This is achieved by keeping the viral load low, which prevents CD4 from decreasing long-term. In acute settings, the major prognostic factor defining mortality is the reason for admission. For patients who are HIV-positive, HAART by itself is not a negative factor defining patient mortality during the ICU stay. The reason for admission is the factor most strongly associated with a poor prognosis. Incorrect Options: Option B - CD4 Count: While the CD4 count is an essential parameter to monitor the immune status and long-term risk of opportunistic infections in HIV patients, it is not the most significant factor predicting a poor prognosis during the patient's current ICU admission. The CD4 count is more relevant in assessing the overall immune function and the risk of developing opportunistic infections over time. In the context of an acute ICU admission, other factors may have a more immediate impact on the patient's prognosis. Option C - Being on HAART therapy: Being on Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART) is actually a positive prognostic factor for HIV-infected patients. HAART has significantly improved the survival and overall health of HIV patients by suppressing viral replication, reducing viral load, and preserving immune function. HAART helps to prevent opportunistic infections and complications associated with advanced HIV disease. Therefore, being on HAART therapy is associated with a better prognosis for HIV patients, especially in the long term. Option D - Age at admission: While age can be a prognostic factor in various medical conditions, in this specific case, the patient's young age of 32 years favors a more favorable outcome. Younger patients generally tend to have better physiological reserves and a more robust immune response, which can positively influence their prognosis. Age alone is not the most significant predictor of a poor prognosis in this HIV-positive patient during her ICU admission. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient says that she doesn’t take her medication regularly. The patient is diagnosed with myocardial infarction and admitted into the hospital. A few hours later, the telemetry monitor shows a second-degree Mobitz type 1 AV block. Her pulse rate is 56/min, BP is 100/60 mmHg and the sugar level is 140 mg/dl. What is the most likely cause of this AV block?

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Inferior wall infarction: This patient with several risk factors (hyperlipidemia and diabetes) suffered from myocardial infarction. ECG strip showed a second-degree heart block. This is most likely due to an inferior wall infarction. An inferior wall MI will show ST elevation in the leads II, III, and aVF. Common presenting symptoms include: Retrosternal chest pain Nausea Diaphoresis Dyspnea The right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the inferior wall of the heart. The SA node is supplied through the branches of RCA. The RCA supplies the AV node through PDA in almost 90% of the people (right dominant circulation). Proximal occlusion of the RCA will result in bradycardia and can also cause AV nodal block. Second and third-degree AV blocks complicating anterior MI carries a poor prognosis. AV block due to MI will resolve in 8-10 days. In symptomatic patients following options are available: IV Atropine (0.6mg) Temporary pacemaker Incorrect Options: Option B- Degenerative changes around the SA node: Degenerative changes around the SA node will result in sick sinus syndrome. ECG findings on the sinoatrial disease can include the following: It is more common in older age and is caused by fibrotic and degenerative changes around the SA node. Patients usually present with syncope, palpitations, and lightheadedness. Permanent pacemaker is the treatment of choice in symptomatic patients. Atrial pacing may prevent episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Option C- Thyrotoxicosis: Thyrotoxicosis is a constellation of symptoms caused due to elevated serum thyroid hormone levels. Some of the important causes are: Grave’s disease Multinodular goiter Toxic adenoma Patients with thyrotoxicosis are more likely to present with atrial fibrillation instead of AV nodal block. Other clinical features include: Weight loss Tachycardia Heat intolerance First-line investigation includes Thyroid profile. TSH receptor antibodies Radioisotope scan Treatment options include: Antithyroid drugs Radioactive iodine Surgery Option D- Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is a medical emergency characterized by: Severe hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dl) Hyperosmolarity (>320 mOsmol/kg) In comparison to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), patients with HHS don’t develop significant ketonuria or acidosis. Hypovolemia will cause reflux tachycardia but not AV block.
