    • Nausea
    • Diaphoresis
    • Dyspnea
  • The right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the inferior wall of the heart.
  • The SA node is supplied through the branches of RCA.
  • The RCA supplies the AV node through PDA in almost 90% of the people (right dominant circulation). Proximal occlusion of the RCA will result in bradycardia and can also cause AV nodal block.
  • Second and third-degree AV blocks complicating anterior MI carries a poor prognosis.

  • AV block due to MI will resolve in 8-10 days. In symptomatic patients following options are available:
  • IV Atropine (0.6mg)
  • Temporary pacemaker

Incorrect Options: 

Option B- Degenerative changes around the SA node:

  • Degenerative changes around the SA node will result in sick sinus syndrome.
  • ECG findings on the sinoatrial disease can include the following:

  • It is more common in older age and is caused by fibrotic and degenerative changes around the SA node.
  • Patients usually present with syncope, palpitations, and lightheadedness.
  • Permanent pacemaker is the treatment of choice in symptomatic patients.
  • Atrial pacing may prevent episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.

Option C- Thyrotoxicosis:

  • Thyrotoxicosis is a constellation of symptoms caused due to elevated serum thyroid hormone levels. Some of the important causes are:
    • Grave’s disease
    • Multinodular goiter
    • Toxic adenoma
  • Patients with thyrotoxicosis are more likely to present with atrial fibrillation instead of AV nodal block.
  • Other clinical features include:
    • Weight loss
    • Tachycardia
    • Heat intolerance
  • First-line investigation includes 
    • Thyroid profile.
    • TSH receptor antibodies
    • Radioisotope scan
  • Treatment options include:
    • Antithyroid drugs
    • Radioactive iodine
    • Surgery

Option D- Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state:

  • Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is a medical emergency characterized by:
    • Severe hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dl)
    • Hyperosmolarity (>320 mOsmol/kg)
  • In comparison to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), patients with HHS don’t develop significant ketonuria or acidosis.
  • Hypovolemia will cause reflux tachycardia but not AV block.
  • Management is done by avoiding rapid changes in serum osmolality:
    • 0.9% normal saline (1L over 1 hour)
    • Insulin infusion
    • Prophylactic heparin

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Complete heart block: Central venous pressure waveform is used to monitor right atrial pressure , and it also gives an overview of the functioning of the right side of the heart. Normal “a-wave” is produced when the atria contracts to push the blood through the healthy tricuspid valve. The waveform in the question stem shows abnormally large “a-waves” known as the cannon “a-waves” , which are seen when atria contracts against the closed AV valves. This situation occurs when there is complete AV dissociation , e.g. In case of complete heart block as seen in this patient. Incorrect Options: Option A- Tricuspid stenosis: Tricuspid stenosis will show prominent/large or giant “a-wave” on the central venous pressure waveform, not the cannon "a-wave." Prominent “a-wave” is due to the forceful atrial contraction against the stenotic tricuspid valve. Option B- Tricuspid regurgitation: Tricuspid regurgitation causes rapid “y” descent ​​​​​​​ Option C- Normal waveform pattern: The waveform shown in the question stem is not the normal waveform pattern. The normal waveform pattern does not produce these abnormally tall "a-waves." ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Only 5-10% of individuals with high levels of alcohol use develop chronic pancreatitis.
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Only 5-10% of individuals with high levels of alcohol use develop chronic pancreatitis: Excessive alcohol consumption is responsible for approximately 70% of cases of chronic pancreatitis, usually after at least 10 years of consumption of 80 to 175 mg of ethanol daily. questions.stem: A 60-year-old male recently diagnosed with AML (M4 variant) is on standard induction therapy with cytarabine (seven day continuous infusion) + an anthracycline (given days 1-3) (7+3 therapy). The patient is paraplegic and is very concerned about developing diarrhea and mucositis during induction therapy. Which of the following medications has been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male recently diagnosed with AML (M4 variant) is on standard induction therapy with cytarabine (seven day continuous infusion) + an anthracycline (given days 1-3) (7+3 therapy). The patient is paraplegic and is very concerned about developing diarrhea and mucositis during induction therapy. Which of the following medications has been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Palifermin: Palifermin is a medication that belongs to the class of keratinocyte growth factors. It plays a crucial role in promoting the growth and repair of epithelial tissues, including the gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa. Patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy regimens, such as those used in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) induction therapy, are at risk of developing severe mucositis and diarrhea due to the damage chemotherapy inflicts on rapidly dividing cells, including those lining the GI tract. Palifermin has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML. A study (Bradstock et al., Br J Haematol 2014) investigated the use of palifermin as prophylaxis against gastrointestinal toxicity after AML induction therapy. The study found that patients who received palifermin had a statistically significant lower rate of grades 3 and 4 gastrointestinal adverse events, primarily due to a reduction in severe diarrhea. While the primary endpoint of reducing grade 3 and 4 oral mucositis was not statistically significant, the study did show evidence of reduced rates of higher grades of oral mucositis in the palifermin arm as well. Incorrect Options: Option A- Zofran (ondansetron): Zofran is an antiemetic medication commonly used to prevent nausea and vomiting associated with chemotherapy. While it helps with nausea and vomiting, it doesn't directly address the issue of severe diarrhea or mucositis in patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy. Option B- Compazine (prochlorperazine): Compazine is also an antiemetic medication that can help manage nausea and vomiting. Like Zofran, it doesn't specifically target mucositis or diarrhea. Option C- Imodium (loperamide): Imodium is an antidiarrheal medication that can be used to manage diarrhea. While it can be helpful in controlling diarrhea symptoms, it doesn't address the underlying issue of mucositis or prevent severe diarrhea in patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Vigabatrin: Vigabatrin is an irreversible inhibitor of GABA transaminase, covalently binding to the enzyme and inactivating it permanently, and is used primarily for infantile spasms in patients with tuberous sclerosis. Its most concerning side effect is concentric vision loss, for which patients taking this medication must be regularly screened. The other medications listed are all reversible inhibitors of their targets: synaptic vesicle protein SV2A for levetiracetam, NMDA receptors for felbamate, GABA transporter for tiagabine, and sodium and calcium channels for valproic acid. Incorrect Options: Option A - Levetiracetam: Levetiracetam is an antiepileptic drug that modulates neurotransmitter release and binds to synaptic vesicle protein SV2A. It does not irreversibly inactivate its target. Option D - Tiagabine: Tiagabine is an antiepileptic drug that inhibits GABA reuptake by blocking the GABA transporter GAT-1. It does not irreversibly inactivate its target. Option E - Valproic acid: Valproic acid is an antiepileptic drug that has multiple mechanisms of action, including increasing GABA levels, blocking sodium channels, and inhibiting certain enzymes. Past medical history is significant for occasional palpitations but less severe than this episode. He does not have any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness. On examination, pulse is notable for irregular rhythm, with a rate of 170 beats per minute. He is vitally stable. His ECG after controlling the rate is given below. Which of the following is the most likely complication his illness can lead to?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Recurrent Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT): The most likely diagnosis in this case scenario is Wolff-Parkinson White (WPW) Syndrome The given ECG shows: A sinus rhythm A rate of 75 beats per min Short PR interval Wide QRS complexes with a slurred delta wave This is consistent with WPW Syndrome. WPW syndrome is an arrhythmia caused by an accessory electrical pathway that bypasses the AV node. The condition is usually congenital and can be associated with other cardiac defects. Symptoms : Most people with WPW syndrome are asymptomatic and are termed to have the WPW pattern on ECG. Some experience a combination of these symptoms: palpitations, tachycardia, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, or syncope and are termed to have WPW syndrome. Diagnosis : ECG : An accessory pathway allows electrical impulses to reach the ventricles more rapidly. Hence causing the characteristic: short PR interval widened QRS complexes delta waves Once the diagnosis is confirmed, other tests are performed to assess the severity of the disease and heart function. Holter monitoring Electrophysiology study Echocardiography Treatment : Medical: Orthodromic AVRT: AV nodal blocking therapy via Vagal maneuvers or drugs such as Beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, Adenosine.[1] Antidromic AVRT and Afib with preexcitation: Rhythm control with procainamide or ibutilide. Catheter ablation : A procedure in which radiofrequency waves are used to destroy the accessory pathway. Surgical : In rare cases, surgery may be required to remove the accessory pathway. Complications : The most common complication of WPW syndrome is recurrent supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Other complications include atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and heart failure. If left untreated, the arrhythmias from WPW syndrome can lead to hemodynamic instability, myocardial infarction and cardiac arrest . Incorrect Options: Options A- Ischemic Stroke: Ischemic stroke is the most common and significant complication of atrial fibrillation (AFib). Although the initial presentation of this patient was most likely due to AFib, it was originally caused by WPW Syndrome as shown in the ECG obtained after sinus rhythm was achieved. Atrial Fibrillation (AFib): In AFib, the disorganized electrical activity causes the atria to quiver instead of normal contraction, which can lead to blood stasis resulting in thrombus formation, stroke, or heart failure. Cause : Atrial Fibrillation can be caused by hypertension, coronary artery disease or myocardial ischemia, valvular defects or congenital heart defects . It can also be caused by an accessory tract such as in WPW which is termed Atrial Fibrillation with preexcitation. It can also be due to hyperthyroidism or other metabolic or endocrine imbalances . It can be due to certain drugs. It is important to find cause to formulate an appropriate management plan. Diagnosis : Electrocardiogram (ECG): Absent P waves Irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm : The disorganized electrical signals from atria cause the ventricles to contract at irregular intervals, hence causing an irregularly irregular rhythm on the ECG. It can be with or without a rapid ventricular response (RVR) Narrow or wide QRS complex : It depends on the underlying conditions of the heart. Holter monitoring: It is used to track cardiac electrical activity over a longer period of time to detect paroxysmal AFib. Echocardiogram to assess the structure and function of the heart. Blood tests: to check for underlying medical conditions or medication side effects. Treatment : Find and treat the underlying cause. Medications: Anticoagulants to prevent blood clots and decrease risk of stroke and Myocardial Infarction. Beta-blockers, or calcium channel blockers to control heart rate. If hemodynamically unstable or refractory to medical management , cardioversion to restore a normal heart rhythm. Ablation therapy to destroy abnormal scar tissue that may be the cause. Surgery , such as a maze procedure, to create scar tissue in the heart to redirect electrical signals. Complications : Stroke or thromboembolism due to impaired blood flow and stasis in the atrial pocket. Heart failure or cardiomyopathy due to prolonged periods of rapid or irregular heart rhythms Fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest pain due to decreased oxygen supply to the body. Option C- Myocardial Infarction (MI): MI occurs as a result of reduced blood flow to cardiac muscles. Any type of arrhythmia, if left untreated for a prolonged period, can cause fatigue and reduce the oxygen flow to cardiac muscles , hence resulting in MI. This is, however, not common as most arrhythmias are diagnosed at an earlier stage due to the appearance of other severe symptoms. Option D- Heart Failure: Arrhythmias can cause heart failure by causing it to pump inefficiently or irregularly , leading to decreased blood flow and oxygen supply to all of the body's organs and tissues. Atrial fibrillation (AFib) is a common arrhythmia that can contribute to the development of heart failure. Chronic arrhythmias that are not well-controlled can lead to structural changes in the heart over time, which can further impair the heart's function and contribute to heart failure. Treatment of arrhythmias either by medication, ablation therapy, or pacemaker implantation, can prevent or manage heart failure.​​​​​​​ @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with a 21-year history of type 1 diabetes with chronic poor control has a most recent HbA1c of 76.0 mmol/mol (9.1%). His current medication includes mealtime short-acting insulin 10-12 units and 15 units of a long-acting insulin analogue in the evening. Retinal screening reveals bilateral background retinopathy and urinalysis reveals albumin:creatinine ratio of 4.9 mg/mmol creat (< 2.5). His main complaint is that of burning discomfort in both feet. Examination of his feet reveals them to be cold but with preserved peripheral pulses and reduced thermosensation, vibration and proprioception sensation. Which of the following would suggest a diagnosis of short fibre neuropathy?
questions.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man with a 21-year history of type 1 diabetes with chronic poor control has a most recent HbA1c of 76.0 mmol/mol (9.1%). His current medication includes mealtime short-acting insulin 10-12 units and 15 units of a long-acting insulin analogue in the evening. Retinal screening reveals bilateral background retinopathy and urinalysis reveals albumin:creatinine ratio of 4.9 mg/mmol creat (&lt; 2.5). His main complaint is that of burning discomfort in both feet. Examination of his feet reveals them to be cold but with preserved peripheral pulses and reduced thermosensation, vibration and proprioception sensation. Which of the following would suggest a diagnosis of short fibre neuropathy?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Reduced thermosensation: Short fibre neuropathy is a later manifestation of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, with symptoms including hyperparesthesia and superficial pain. Incorrect Option: Option B - Decreased light pressure sensation: It is not characteristic of short fiber neuropathy. Decreased light pressure sensation is associated with large fiber neuropathy, which primarily affects the large myelinated nerve fibers responsible for conveying touch and proprioceptive sensations. Option C - Diminished ankle jerks: It is more indicative of large fiber neuropathy, which can lead to reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes, including ankle jerks. Option D - Paraesthesia: It is a common feature of diabetic neuropathy, but it is not specific to short fiber neuropathy. Paraesthesia refers to abnormal sensations like tingling, burning, or prickling and can be present in both large and small fiber neuropathy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with muscle weakness, fasciculations, cramps, and sweating. Her medications include pyridostigmine 120mg TID (recently increased from 60mg BID) and lamotrigine (recently increased from 25 to 50mg per day) for a mood disorder. She works from home while raising her young children, and she and her children have been in good health. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman presents with muscle weakness, fasciculations, cramps, and sweating. Her medications include pyridostigmine 120mg TID (recently increased from 60mg BID) and lamotrigine (recently increased from 25 to 50mg per day) for a mood disorder. She works from home while raising her young children, and she and her children have been in good health. What is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Pyridostigmine: Pyridostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor commonly used to treat myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular disorder characterized by muscle weakness and fatigue. In a cholinergic crisis, an excessive dose or overdose of cholinesterase inhibitors can lead to an exaggerated cholinergic effect, resulting in symptoms such as muscle weakness, fasciculations (muscle twitching), cramps, and sweating. The dramatic increase in the patient's pyridostigmine dose from 120mg/day to 360mg/day may have contributed to the development of the cholinergic crisis. Management involves stopping the cholinesterase inhibitor and providing supportive care, and the patient's symptoms should resolve with time. Incorrect Options: Option A - Lamotrigine: Lamotrigine is an antiepileptic medication commonly used for mood disorders and epilepsy. While it can have side effects, worsening muscle weakness, fasciculations, and cramps are not typical side effects of lamotrigine. In this case, the patient's symptoms are more consistent with cholinergic crisis, which is associated with excessive use of cholinesterase inhibitors like pyridostigmine. Option B - Infection: While infections can cause a variety of symptoms, including muscle weakness and cramps, they are not typically associated with fasciculations and sweating. Additionally, the patient and her children have been in good health, which makes an acute infectious process less likely as the cause of her symptoms. Option D - Toxic exposure: Toxic exposures can indeed cause a range of neurological symptoms, but in this case, the patient's symptoms are more closely related to the use of pyridostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor. Toxic exposures would usually cause more generalized symptoms and may not explain the specific pattern of muscle weakness, fasciculations, cramps, and sweating observed in this patient. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml:
A 48-year-old male patient who has undergone Nissen fundoplication 9 months ago is complaining of dysphagia to solid foods for the past 12 weeks, with occasional regurgitation. He describes a sensation of something “sticking” in the lower chest. He denies heartburn. Preoperatively, esophageal motility studies were normal, and pH studies revealed persistent acidic reflux despite maximal PPI therapy. He has been off PPI therapy since surgery.
A radiographic study shows that the patient passes a swallowed barium tablet through the esophagus successfully but more slowly than expected. Which of the following is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Upper endoscopy with dilation: Dysphagia occurs in most patients to some degree after surgery, requiring a modified dietary intake of liquids for up to 12 weeks. After 12 weeks, persistent dysphagia should be evaluated. Patients who pass a barium tablet slowly through the esophagus and who have normal preoperative esophageal motility are candidates for dilation. Up to 12% of patients required dilation after fundoplication in several studies. Dilation is usually performed over a guidewire or directly with a bougie, with or without endoscopic visualization. Incorrect Options: Option A - Trial of PPI therapy: Patients with persistent dysphagia after 12 weeks should be evaluated to determine if dilation is indicated before beginning antisecretory therapy. Option B - Trial of metoclopramide: An empiric trial of metoclopramide may be useful in some patients with postoperative bloating. Option C - Esophageal manometry and pH-impedance studies: Esophageal pH-impedance studies may be useful to assess a subset of patients who have persistent symptoms without clear evidence of esophageal dysfunction. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Trientine: The patient’s findings suggest a diagnosis of Wilson’s disease. Wilson disease is a disorder characterized by the absence of a copper-transporting membrane ATPase pump in the trans-Golgi network of hepatocytes, which prevents the elimination of copper, resulting in accumulation in hepatic lysosomes. It is characterized by low circulating levels of ceruloplasmin. Since ceruloplasmin typically contains 95% of circulating copper, total plasma copper is typically low. Free plasma copper is increased. Treatment of Wilson disease attempts to mobilize and enhance the elimination of excess copper and to prevent further copper absorption. Trientine is the first line of treatment, with dietary restriction of foods high in copper and prevention of absorption by treatment with oral zinc. Incorrect Options: Option A - Prednisone: Prednisone is used for the treatment of autoimmune hepatitis. Option C - Entecavir: Entecavir is used for the treatment of chronic active HBV infection. questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of severe shortness of breath. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. Spirometry is performed and forced expiratory volume in the first second after the bronchodilator is 65% of the predictive value. A clinical diagnosis of emphysema is made. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor which is synthesised by the liver. questions.stem: A 70-year-old male with a known case of asthma presents with a PaCO2 of 60 mmHg. Assuming he has chronic CO2 retention (and no other systemic illness), his arterial blood gas sample will demonstrate a bicarbonate of which value?
questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old male with a known case of asthma presents with a PaCO2 of 60 mmHg. Assuming he has chronic CO2 retention (and no other systemic illness), his arterial blood gas sample will demonstrate a bicarbonate of which value?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - 32mEq/L: Homeostasis by adjusting the final pH of the blood. Respiratory CO2 retention is compensated by increased serum bicarbonate concentration via renal retention of bicarbonate. Compensatory mechanisms are more efficient in chronic states than in acute state. For increased CO2 in blood, expected bicarbonate can be calculated as follows: chronic compensation expected HCO3 = 0.4 (CO2-40) + 24. This formula assumes normal CO2 to be 40 mmHg and normal bicarbonate to be 24mEq/L. For this patient, expected bicarbonate = 0.4(60-40) + 24 = 32. Incorrect Options: Option A - 28 mEq/L: This value would be appropriate for acute retention of CO2, not chronic. The formula for acute CO2 retention compensation is: 0.2(CO2-40) + 24. For this patient with a PaCO2 of 60 mmHg, the expected bicarbonate level would be 0.2(60-40) + 24 = 28 mEq/L. Option B - 16 mEq/L: This patient has respiratory acidosis, and in response, the compensatory mechanism would be metabolic alkalosis. A bicarbonate level of 16 mEq/L would be indicative of metabolic acidosis, which would exacerbate the acidosis rather than compensate for it. Option D - 40 mEq/L: This value is more than the expected compensation. If the bicarbonate level were found to be 40 mEq/L in this patient with a PaCO2 of 60 mmHg, it would suggest an additional metabolic alkalosis, which is not part of the compensation for respiratory acidosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl visits the doctor after experiencing nausea, increased urinary frequency, and breast tenderness for three weeks. She has never had a menstrual cycle. She is an active member of her school's track and field squad. Her height is 173 cm (5 feet 8 in), and her weight is 54 kg (120 lb); her BMI is 18 kg/m2. Tanner's stage 5 breast and pubic hair growth. Which of the following serum tests is the most suitable next step in this patient's diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl visits the doctor after experiencing nausea, increased urinary frequency, and breast tenderness for three weeks. She has never had a menstrual cycle. She is an active member of her school's track and field squad. Her height is 173 cm (5 feet 8 in), and her weight is 54 kg (120 lb); her BMI is 18 kg/m2. Tanner's stage 5 breast and pubic hair growth. Which of the following serum tests is the most suitable next step in this patient's diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Human chorionic gonadotropin: The patient presents with primary amenorrhoea and pregnancy symptoms. To determine conception, a human chorionic gonadotropin assay is used. β-hCG can be detected in blood 6-9 days after fertilisation (or in urine 14 days later). Aside from amenorrhea, other early clinical characteristics of pregnancy include nausea and vomiting, desires for or aversions to certain foods, breast enlargement and tenderness, polyuria, areola hyperpigmentation, and bluish cervix discolouration. Although this 16-year-old girl has not yet had her first menstruation period, pregnancy should be ruled out before proceeding with other diagnostic procedures. Incorrect Options: Option B - Oestriol: Normal pregnancy results in a 1000-fold rise in oestriol levels. However, estriol, which starts to rise only in the eighth and ninth weeks of pregnancy, has a low sensitivity and specificity for early pregnancy diagnosis. Instead, oestriol monitors fetal health; a low estriol level during the second trimester can suggest congenital disabilities such as Down syndrome. Option C - Thyrotropin: Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) or thyrotropin levels are measured to identify thyroid disorders. Amenorrhea is a symptom of hyperthyroidism. Because of damage to the posterior pituitary gland, a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, a secondary hyperthyroidism source, can also produce nausea and increased urinary frequency. Breast tenderness, on the other hand, would not be caused by hyperthyroidism or pituitary injury. Other symptoms, such as heat intolerance, diaphoresis, insomnia, and restlessness, would be anticipated, but none are present in this patient. Option D - Luteinising hormone: Luteinising hormone (LH) levels are measured in patients with primary amenorrhea to distinguish hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and to identify androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS). Female teenagers participating in athletic activities can develop a functional hypothalamic disturbance (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism), but breast and pubic hair development is also delayed in adolescent hypogonadism. Total AIS would result in age-appropriate breast development, as seen here, but patients with total AIS would not acquire pubic hair. LH values are not used to determine pregnancy status. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Mitofusin-2 has which of the following functions?
questions.stemHtml: Mitofusin-2 has which of the following functions?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Mitochondrial transport: Mitofusin-2 plays a role in mitochondrial transport and fusion. Mutations in the gene encoding this protein (MFN2) are associated with autosomal dominant axonal Charcot-Marie Tooth disease (CMT2A). The polymerase-γ enzyme (encoded by POLG) is the only polymerase involved in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) replication, and also plays a role in mtDNA repair. As a result, impaired function of the enzyme leads to mitochondrial DNA depletion. With mtDNA depletion there is a reduction in mtDNA-encoded proteins such as tRNAs and rRNAs, followed by impaired ATP synthesis and therefore impaired cellular function and survival. As with other mitochondrial disorders, the disorder is likely to manifest with dysfunction in tissues/organ systems with elevated basal energy requirements (e.g., CNS and PNS, cardiac, skeletal muscle, and GI). Both thymidine kinase-2 (gene = TK2) and thymidine phosphorylase (gene = TYMP) are enzymes that play a role in phosphorylation of thymidine (in different pathways), and mutations in the genes encoding these proteins are associated with mitochondrial DNA depletion myopathy and mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalomyopathy (MNGIE), respectively. Incorrect Options: Option A - Mitochondrial DNA replication: Mitofusin-2 (MFN2) is not directly involved in mitochondrial DNA replication. DNA replication in mitochondria is primarily regulated by enzymes and proteins specific to the mitochondrial genome. Option B - Mitochondrial DNA repair: MFN2 is not directly involved in mitochondrial DNA repair. DNA repair processes in mitochondria are carried out by specific proteins and enzymes that are responsible for maintaining the integrity of the mitochondrial genome. Option D - Phosphorylation of deoxyribonucleosides: MFN2 is not involved in the phosphorylation of deoxyribonucleosides. Phosphorylation of deoxyribonucleosides is a cellular process carried out by various kinases and is essential for DNA synthesis and repair. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Overabundance of fat cells within the marrow space
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Overabundance of fat cells within the marrow space: Aplastic anemia (AA) is characterized by a bone marrow that is hypocellular, meaning that there is a decrease in the number of hematopoietic stem cells. As the marrow becomes devoid of these stem cells, it gets replaced by fat cells, leading to an overabundance of fat cells within the marrow space. This is a distinguishing feature when considering a diagnosis of AA over hypoplastic MDS. Incorrect Options: Option A - Multiple cytogenetic abnormalities : This is more suggestive of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) rather than aplastic anemia. MDS is a clonal disorder where there's an aberration in the DNA of the hematopoietic stem cells, which may manifest as multiple cytogenetic abnormalities. Option B - Multi-lineage dysplasia: Multi-lineage dysplasia is characteristic of MDS. In MDS, there is dysplasia, or abnormal maturation, of cells from multiple hematopoietic lineages, including red cells, white cells, and platelets. This feature helps distinguish MDS from AA, where dysplasia isn't a hallmark feature. questions.answerText: The Mayo risk score is useful for assessment of prognosis.
questions.solution: Correct Option D - The Mayo risk score is useful for assessment of prognosis: This patient’s presentation is consistent with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), which refers to a chronic progressive disorder characterized by inflammation, fibrosis, and medium- and large-duct strictures in the extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts. There is a strong association with IBD, and most (up to 90%) patients have underlying ulcerative colitis, although PSC occurs in approximately 5% of patients with UC and in a smaller percentage of patients with Crohn disease. Clinical presentation may be characterized by fatigue and pruritus or may be normal. Exam is often normal, although excoriations due to pruritus, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and jaundice may be seen. Liver enzymes show a cholestatic pattern of abnormality, with elevation of alkaline phosphatase in most patients. Ultrasound findings include bile duct abnormalities, including wall thickening, dilations, and strictures. Serum immunoglobulin M levels are increased in up to 50% of patients and p-ANCA is present in 30% to 90% of patients. The Mayo risk score is a validated statistical model that incorporates age, serum bilirubin, serum AST, and history of variceal bleeding to assess prognosis. Incorrect Option: Option A - Liver biopsy is indicated for diagnosis: Liver biopsy is rarely diagnostic but may be used for staging the disease. It may be used to confirm the diagnosis if cholangiography does not display characteristic bile duct changes, including multifocal strictures and segmental dilations. Option B - It is the most frequent extrapancreatic manifestation of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis: IgG4 cholangitis is the most common extrapancreatic manifestation of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis and rarely occurs in the absence of pancreatitis. Option C - He does not have an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma: Patients with PSC and cirrhosis have an increased risk of HCC, although HCC is not as common as with other causes of cirrhosis. Biopsy or transient elastography can be used to assess fibrosis, which occurs as the disease progresses. Patients with PSC have a 10-15% lifetime risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma (CCA). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Patient is a 27-year-old male who presents to the emergency room with palpitations for one day. Patient is tremulous but oriented and complaining of abdominal pain and diarrhea. Patient is afebrile. Blood pressure is 100/78 mmHg with a heart rate of 125 beats per minute. Patient has proptosis bilaterally. What should be avoided in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: Patient is a 27-year-old male who presents to the emergency room with palpitations for one day. Patient is tremulous but oriented and complaining of abdominal pain and diarrhea. Patient is afebrile. Blood pressure is 100/78 mmHg with a heart rate of 125 beats per minute. Patient has proptosis bilaterally. What should be avoided in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - IV contrast: Patient is suffering from thyrotoxicosis but can have worsening symptoms if a large dose of iodine is given, especially before a thionamide antithyroid drug is given. The concern is for Jod-Basedow phenomenon . This can cause enhanced thyroid hormone synthesis, enrich hormone stores within the gland, and thereby permit further exaggeration of thyrotoxicosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - IV fluids : Patient has thyrotoxicosis from Graves' disease. IV fluids would be appropriate as these patients are at risk for fluid depletion from hyperpyrexia, diaphoresis, vomiting, or diarrhea. Also, dehydration could be contributing to his tachycardia. Option B and C - (Atenolol & Propranolo) : Usage of beta-blockers not only corrects the heart rate and decreases the oxygen demand of cardiac muscle, but also improves agitation, convulsions, psychotic behaviour, tremor, diarrhoea, fever, and diaphoresis. Either atenolol or metoprolol can be used. @Neet_pg_bot

Her observed vitals in the ER are BP: 130/90, Pulse: 120/min, RR:32/min, Temp: 98oF and SpO2: 92%. On examination, she has pedal oedema with ascites and hepatomegaly. Which of the following is the best intervention for the following patient which will provide immediate relief to patients PAH?

On examination, she has pedal oedema with ascites and hepatomegaly. Her right heart catheterization pressure confirmed pulmonary arterial hypertension on the background of pulmonary Embolism. options.label: A

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Thromboendarterectomy Pulmonary hypertension is defined as elevated mean pulmonary pressure beyond 20 mmHg or pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 15 mmHg or less or pulmonary vascular resistance of 3 Wood units or more. This particular patient belongs to Group IV hypertension according to WHO Classification. This group consists of patients with pulmonary hypertension due to thromboembolic occlusion of the proximal and distal pulmonary arteries. Furthermore, she is suffering from NYHA Class IV Pulmonary hypertension with the inability to perform any physical activity without symptoms. She has evidence of right heart failure, dyspnea and fatigue at rest and worsening of symptoms with any activity. Since this patient has developed Pulmonary Embolism, no other therapy is going to relieve the patient’s symptoms except thromboendarterectomy which will provide quick relief of PAH and resulting symptoms Incorrect Options: Option A - Supplemental oxygen for 15 hours or more per day Long-term oxygen therapy is recommended for patients with WHO Group III pulmonary hypertension (due to lung disease) and hypoxemia at rest or with physical activity. In patients with COPD and hypoxemia, the administration of supplemental oxygen for 15 hours or more per day has been shown to slow the progression of pulmonary hypertension. The patient does not belong to WHO Classification Group III. Option B - Oral endothelin receptor antagonists The preferred treatment for WHO Group I patients and NYHA class II pulmonary arterial hypertension include oral endothelin receptor antagonists (ambrisentan, bosentan, macitentan), phosphodiesterase inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil), and soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators (riociguat). WHO Group I Pulmonary hypertension consists of diseases that affect the pulmonary arteries and cause structural changes, smooth muscle hypertrophy, and endothelial dysfunction for example idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension, connective tissue disorders, congenital heart disease NYHA Class II: Pulmonary hypertension resulting in slight limitation of physical activity. No symptoms at rest but ordinary physical activity causes dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, or near syncope. The patient belongs neither to Group 1 hypertension nor to Class II. Option C - Diuretics and ACE inhibitors Treatment of patients with Group II pulmonary hypertension (secondary to left heart failure) has the main goal of decreasing pulmonary venous pressure by treating heart failure and volume overload. The patient does not have Group II hypertension. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Stage IV squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, mild MDS, ECOG=1
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Stage IV squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, mild MDS, ECOG=1 Cisplatin and carboplatin are both platinum-based chemotherapy agents, but they have different toxicity profiles. Cisplatin can cause nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity, which makes carboplatin a more suitable option in some patients. In the case of a patient with mild MDS (myelodysplastic syndrome), who already has some degree of bone marrow dysfunction, carboplatin might be chosen over cisplatin to reduce the risk of further exacerbating the marrow dysfunction. Incorrect Options: Option A - Stage II nonseminomatous germ cell tumor 1st line treatment: Cisplatin has shown superior outcomes in testicular cancer and is usually preferred in this setting. Option C - Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder, neoadjuvant: Cisplatin is generally considered superior to carboplatin in the treatment of transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy has shown improved survival rates in muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Option D - Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder, adjuvant: Again, cisplatin has demonstrated superior outcomes to carboplatin in the treatment of bladder cancer, and is generally the preferred agent. Adjuvant cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy can improve survival in patients with high-risk muscle-invasive bladder cancer post-surgery. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia and migraines with visual aura presents to the emergency department after he developed sudden vision loss in his right eye yesterday evening. At first, he attributed it to a new manifestation of a migraine and did not immediately seek medical attention. He presents to the ED this evening as his vision loss has not resolved. He takes atenolol and simvastatin. On exam, BP is 150/90 mmHg, HR is 77 beats/minute, RR are 14 breaths/minute. Cardiovascular exam is significant for a carotid bruit. A stroke protocol is activated. CT head returns negative for acute stroke. A funduscopic exam demonstrates whitening of the retina in the right eye. Of the following, what is the next best step in clinical management?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia and migraines with visual aura presents to the emergency department after he developed sudden vision loss in his right eye yesterday evening. At first, he attributed it to a new manifestation of a migraine and did not immediately seek medical attention. He presents to the ED this evening as his vision loss has not resolved. He takes atenolol and simvastatin. On exam, BP is 150/90 mmHg, HR is 77 beats/minute, RR are 14 breaths/minute. Cardiovascular exam is significant for a carotid bruit. A stroke protocol is activated. CT head returns negative for acute stroke. A funduscopic exam demonstrates whitening of the retina in the right eye. Of the following, what is the next best step in clinical management?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Optimize cardiovascular risk factors: The vignette describes a patient presenting with a retinal artery occlusion. In a patient with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia, an embolic event is highest on the differential. A stroke protocol should be activated. There is no definitive treatment for a retinal artery occlusion, particularly if outside of the six-hour window when re-perfusion measures are most effective. Intra-arterial thrombolysis, ocular massage, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy are all measures that have been used with inconclusive evidence for efficacy. The best next step in management is to optimize a patient’s cardiovascular risk factors, which include controlling blood pressure, lipid levels, glucose levels, and screening for atherosclerosis. Incorrect Options: Option B - Intra-arterial thrombolysis: tPA has not been conclusively shown to be effective in the management of a central retinal artery occlusion, and is not without risk (i.e. intracranial bleeding). Observational studies to date lack strong supportive evidence. Additionally, the time window from symptom onset (greater than 6 hours) in this vignette decreases the likelihood that any reperfusion technique would be effective. Option C - Ocular massage: Ocular massage is thought to assist in dislodging embolus farther down the arterial circulation with the goal of improving retinal perfusion. However, no clinical studies have shown conclusive evidence that ocular massage results in improved visual outcomes. Option D - Hyperbaric oxygen: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy has been shown in a few case reports to restore oxygen to the retina if done within 24 hours of symptoms. It involves breathing pure oxygen in a pressured room or tube. However, this patient is out of the 24 hour window and therefore this is not the best next step in clinical management. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 19 year old male patient k/c/o beta thalassemia presents to you with h/o numerous blood transfusions, and says that he has never been on iron chelation. Which of the following ferritin targets is appropriate to start considering chelation therapy for patients with beta-thalassemia?
questions.stemHtml: A 19 year old male patient k/c/o beta thalassemia presents to you with h/o numerous blood transfusions, and says that he has never been on iron chelation. Which of the following ferritin targets is appropriate to start considering chelation therapy for patients with beta-thalassemia?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - 1,000 to 1,500 ng/mL: Patients with beta-thalassemia, particularly those receiving frequent blood transfusions, are at risk of developing iron overload due to both increased gastrointestinal iron absorption and the iron content of packed red blood cell transfusions. Iron overload can lead to serious complications, including damage to the liver, heart, and other organs. Iron chelation therapy is a key management strategy to prevent or reduce iron overload in patients with thalassemia. Chelation therapy involves using medications that bind to excess iron in the body, allowing it to be excreted and preventing its accumulation in organs. The appropriate ferritin target for starting iron chelation therapy in patients with beta-thalassemia is generally considered to be between 1,000 and 1,500 ng/mL. Ferritin is a marker of iron storage in the body, and levels above this range indicate significant iron overload. Initiating chelation therapy within this range helps prevent the accumulation of iron in organs and reduces the risk of complications such as liver fibrosis, cardiac dysfunction, and endocrine abnormalities. Incorrect Options: Option A - 200 ng/mL to 500 ng/mL: Ferritin levels in this range are generally not considered high enough to warrant immediate iron chelation therapy. However, ongoing monitoring is important as levels may increase over time. Option B - 500 to 1,000 ng/mL: While ferritin levels in this range are higher and indicate some degree of iron overload, the risk of complications is higher when levels exceed 1,000 ng/mL, especially in patients with beta-thalassemia major. Option D - 2,500 to 5,000 ng/mL: Ferritin levels in this range represent significant iron overload, and chelation therapy is typically initiated before levels reach this point to prevent complications. Waiting for ferritin levels to exceed 2,500 ng/mL before starting chelation therapy could lead to irreversible organ damage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with a history of obesity, diabetes, and hypertension presents with 2 days of a productive cough, a fever, and shortness of breath. Her cough is productive with thick, yellow sputum. At baseline, she walks 2 miles every day. However, the patient can now walk only half of a block, stopping because of dyspnea. On physical examination, she has a temperature of 38.4°C, blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg, heart rate 115/minute, respiratory rate 28/minute, and oxygen saturation 85% while breathing room air. Her oxygen saturation improves to only 87% when supplemental oxygen is administered with a 100% non-rebreather mask. She appears in mild respiratory distress and is speaking in short sentences. Cardiac exam is notably for tachycardia. No murmurs are appreciated. Chest exam reveals bronchial breath sounds with egophony at the right base. Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender. She does not have lower extremity edema. What is the pathophysiologic mechanism of this patient’s hypoxemia?

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Shunt: The five pathophysiologic mechanisms for hypoxemia include hypoventilation, decreased partial pressure of inspired oxygen, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, shunt, and diffusion impairment. Shunt is the only cause of hypoxemia where the oxygen saturation does not significantly improve after the administration of supplemental oxygen. Incorrect Options: Option A - Diffusion impairment: Diffusion impairment refers to a problem in the transfer of oxygen from the alveoli of the lungs into the bloodstream. This can occur in conditions such as pulmonary fibrosis. In diffusion impairment, oxygen saturation improves with the administration of supplemental oxygen because more oxygen is available in the alveoli for diffusion into the blood. Option B - Hypoventilation: Hypoventilation refers to a decrease in the amount of air entering the alveoli of the lungs. This can be caused by various conditions, including respiratory depression due to drugs or neuromuscular diseases. In hypoventilation, oxygen saturation improves with the administration of supplemental oxygen because more oxygen is available for diffusion into the blood. Option C - Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch refers to an imbalance between the amount of air reaching the alveoli (ventilation) and the amount of blood flowing through the capillaries surrounding the alveoli (perfusion). V/Q mismatch can occur in conditions such as pneumonia or pulmonary embolism. In V/Q mismatch, oxygen saturation improves with the administration of supplemental oxygen because more oxygen is available for diffusion into the blood. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: You consult a 63-year-old gentleman with a history of atrial fibrillation, on warfarin, who is hemodynamically unstable from a bleeding undiagnosed esophageal varices, requiring significant resuscitation with crystalloids as well as packed RBCs. You decide to order 3 factor aPCC. Which of the following coagulation factors is NOT found in 3-factor PCC?
questions.stemHtml: You consult a 63-year-old gentleman with a history of atrial fibrillation, on warfarin, who is hemodynamically unstable from a bleeding undiagnosed esophageal varices, requiring significant resuscitation with crystalloids as well as packed RBCs. You decide to order 3 factor aPCC. Which of the following coagulation factors is NOT found in 3-factor PCC?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Factor VII: Three-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (3-factor PCC) contains factors II (prothrombin), IX, and X. This combination of factors is used to help correct clotting deficiencies in patients with bleeding disorders, especially those on warfarin therapy who require rapid reversal of anticoagulation. However, factor VII is not present in 3-factor PCC. Factor VII is included in four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4-factor PCC), which contains factors II, VII, IX, and X. 4-factor PCC is often used in patients with significant bleeding or those who require urgent reversal of anticoagulation, as it provides a more comprehensive replacement of clotting factors. Incorrect Options: Option A - Factor IX: Factor IX is present in both 3-factor and 4-factor PCC. It plays a crucial role in the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade. Option C - Factor X: Factor X is present in both 3-factor and 4-factor PCC. It is a key factor in the common pathway of the coagulation cascade, where it converges with both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. Option D - Factor II (Prothrombin): Factor II, also known as prothrombin, is present in both 3-factor and 4-factor PCC. It is converted into thrombin during the coagulation process, leading to the conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin, which forms the clot. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents to your urgent care following a suspected bite by "something in the woodpile." He says is it happened a few hours ago while he was getting wood, when he suddenly felt a pain in his finger and pulled back. Initially it stung, but now several hours later it is hurting more, swelling, and getting black and blue. He feels well otherwise and has no past medical history. His tetanus is up-to-date. His vitals upon arrival are BP 125/85 mmHg, HR 100 beats/minute, RR 16 breaths/minute, temperature 98.8 degrees Fahrenheit, and O2 saturation 99% on RA. Upon exam you see his finger as below. What is the most important aspect of management for this injury?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man presents to your urgent care following a suspected bite by "something in the woodpile." His vitals upon arrival are BP 125/85 mmHg, HR 100 beats/minute, RR 16 breaths/minute, temperature 98.8 degrees Fahrenheit, and O2 saturation 99% on RA. Upon exam you see his finger as below. What is the most important aspect of management for this injury?

options.label: A
options.text: Soak it in betadine and open up the eschar

options.label: C
options.text: Clean it up and then dress it with gauze that is soaked with Vaseline before starting the patient on a course of a cephalosporin

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Immediate transfer to the ER: This is a pit viper bite with envenomation . Copperheads and sometimes rattlesnakes are found in wood piles. When a crotalid viper envenomates (which is only 20-25% of the time), the initial wound may appear subtle, however, over several hours it will swell and show hemorrhage and eschar . Untreated, significant systemic coagulopathy can develop along with tissue necrosis. He needs immediate ER transfer for evaluation and consideration of crotalid antivenom . Brown recluse spiders also live in wood piles and their bites result in local effects, tissue necrosis, and occasional systemic effects. The effects of recluse spider envenomation do not progress this rapidly and envenomation is not associated with hemorrhage. It is important to recognize snake envenomation so it can be treated rapidly before progression. Incorrect Options: Option A - Soak it in betadine and open up the eschar: Soak it in betadine and open up the eschar: Opening up the eschar or attempting to manipulate the wound in this manner can potentially worsen the injury, introduce infection, and increase the risk of complications. Immediate transfer to the ER is the priority for proper evaluation and management of pit viper envenomation. Option C - Clean it up and then dress it with gauze that is soaked with Vaseline before starting the patient on a course of a cephalosporin : Clean it up and then dress it with gauze that is soaked with Vaseline before starting the patient on a course of a cephalosporin: While wound cleaning and dressing are important steps, the immediate priority in this case is to recognize and manage the potential pit viper bite. Prompt transfer to the ER is crucial for proper evaluation, potential administration of antivenom, and appropriate management of envenomation. Option D - Start the patient on dapsone : Start the patient on dapsone: Dapsone is used in the treatment of brown recluse spider bites, not pit viper envenomation. Brown recluse spider bites can lead to tissue necrosis and other local effects, but they do not typically cause the rapid progression, swelling, and hemorrhage seen in pit viper envenomation. Immediate transfer to the ER is the appropriate action in this case. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Admit to ICU and commence resuscitation with IV fluid and blood transfusion
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Admit to ICU and commence resuscitation with IV fluid and blood transfusion: This patient presentation is consistent with decompensated cirrhosis, and upper GI bleeding from gastric or esophageal varices as a result of portal hypertension is the most likely etiology. questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the processes of ACQUIRED peripheral nervous system demyelination with remyelination is true?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements regarding the processes of ACQUIRED peripheral nervous system demyelination with remyelination is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Demyelination with remyelination results in an increased internodal distance

options.label: B
options.text: Demyelination with remyelination has no effect on the internodal distance

options.label: C
options.text: Demyelination with remyelination results in a decreased internodal distance

options.label: D
options.text: Demyelination with complete remyelination will return conduction velocities to the pre-injury baseline values

questions.answerText: Demyelination with remyelination results in a decreased internodal distance
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Demyelination with remyelination results in a decreased internodal distance: Once demyelination is complete, remyelination can take place. However, remyelination will result in internodal distances comparable to those that were laid down when the axon was originally myelinated as a child. Note that the number of internodes does not change between childhood and adulthood, and therefore as limbs grow so does the internodal distance. As a result of these shortened internodes, covering the previously demyelinated segment, conduction velocities across the segment will be slower (i.e., more nodes over the same distance will have to be depolarized during salutatory conduction). Therefore, only answer option c is correct. Incorrect Options: Option A - Demyelination with remyelination results in an increased internodal distance: Demyelination with subsequent remyelination does not lead to an increased internodal distance. In fact, the internodal distance remains relatively constant during the remyelination process. Option B - Demyelination with remyelination has no effect on the internodal distance: Demyelination and remyelination can affect the internodal distance, especially in cases where remyelination is incomplete or if there are aberrant processes involved. Option D - Demyelination with complete remyelination will return conduction velocities to the pre-injury baseline values: While remyelination does improve nerve conduction velocity, it may not always return to the exact pre-injury baseline values. The extent of recovery depends on various factors, including the extent of remyelination and the level of damage to the axons and underlying nerve structures. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - At the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery: One of the most feared and deadly neuro-ophthalmic emergencies, acute 3rd nerve palsy from aneurysm is important to remember both for clinical reasons and for test taking reasons. While saccular aneurysms can occur virtually anywhere in the cerebral circulation, aneurysms at the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery often present with a pupil involving 3rd nerve palsy by compressing the 3rd nerve as it passes by in the subarachnoid space. The parasympathetic fibers responsible for contraction of the pupillary sphincter muscle (resulting in pupillary constriction) travel in the peripheral segment of the 3rd nerve and are therefore very vulnerable to external compression. Microvascular 3rd nerve palsies can rarely have pupil involvement but it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after a thorough evaluation to rule out an aneurysm. Pupil involvement is typically defined as more than 1 mm of anisocoria measured in room light. The anisocoria should be greater in bright light conditions and the pupil is often poorly responsive to direct light and also shows a poor consensual response (when light is shined in the contralateral eye). questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of kidney disease undergoes a renal function test to assess his kidney function. Which of the following tests measures the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man with a history of kidney disease undergoes a renal function test to assess his kidney function. Which of the following tests measures the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Inulin clearance: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is a measure of how well the kidneys filter waste products and excess fluids from the blood. It is considered the most accurate way to assess kidney function. Inulin is a substance that is freely filtered by the glomeruli and is not reabsorbed or secreted by the renal tubules, making it an ideal marker for GFR measurement. Inulin clearance is a test that involves injecting a known amount of inulin into the bloodstream and then measuring the amount of inulin that is excreted in the urine over a specified period of time. This allows for calculation of the GFR. Other tests, such as blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine, can provide indirect measures of kidney function but are less accurate than GFR measurement using inulin clearance. BUN is a measure of the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood and can be affected by factors such as dehydration, diet, and liver function, making it less specific for kidney function. questions.stem: You are attempting to better understand how genetic variations of various cytochrome P-450 enzymes affects oestrogen metabolism and ultimately impacts breast cancer incidence. You discover that this is due to a microsatellite variation with a 4 base pair sequence repetition within a P-450 enzyme gene. This is an example of what genetic principle?
questions.stemHtml: You are attempting to better understand how genetic variations of various cytochrome P-450 enzymes affects oestrogen metabolism and ultimately impacts breast cancer incidence. You discover that this is due to a microsatellite variation with a 4 base pair sequence repetition within a P-450 enzyme gene. This is an example of what genetic principle?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Genetic polymorphism: This example demonstrates a genetic polymorphism which results in a variant that affects oestrogen metabolism, ultimately putting the patient at a higher risk of developing breast cancer. In genetics, polymorphism is when multiple (more than 2) alleles can occupy a gene locus in the population. A polymorphic variant of a gene can be related to a disease, such as cancer. Genetic polymorphisms can occur due to a deletion or a duplication of a DNA base pair sequence. Both SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) and microsatellite variations are examples of polymorphisms. It is thought that genetic polymorphisms play a much larger role in cancer risk than high-penetrance mutations in tumour suppressor genes or oncogenes, which are more rare. Incorrect Options: Option A - Epigenetic silencing: Epigenetic silencing is a genetic term that refers to how a gene's expression is regulated. Typically, expression of a gene can be silenced by methylation or hypermethylation. There is published evidence of promoter CpG island hypermethylation driving the transcriptional repression of tumour-suppressor genes and ultimately leading to malignancy (Esteller., Hum Mol Genet 2007). Option C - Incomplete penetrance: Incomplete penetrance refers to a situation where not all individuals who carry a certain gene will express the symptom or trait associated with that gene. Option D - Genetic imprinting: Genetic imprinting, or genome imprinting, is when a gene expression varies depending on whether it was inherited from the father or the mother. There are ~75 examples that occur in humans. In medicine, an example of imprinting can be seen in Prader-Willi syndrome versus Angelman syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis associated with hepatitis C infection is evaluated for confusion. Exam reveals asterixis, ascites, and a sweet odour to his breath. Which of the following is true?
questions.stemHtml: A patient with cirrhosis associated with hepatitis C infection is evaluated for confusion. Exam reveals asterixis, ascites, and a sweet odour to his breath. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The serum ammonia level correlates with the severity of hepatic encephalopathy

options.label: B
options.text: The diagnosis is made by electroencephalograph

options.label: C
options.text: Precipitants for this condition are present in over 80% of patients

options.label: D
options.text: TIPS placement is a second-line treatment

questions.answerText: Precipitants for this condition are present in over 80% of patients
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Precipitants for this condition are present in over 80% of patients: Hepatic encephalopathy is characterized by asterixis, although a distal tremor may be present in early stages. Some patients may have a sweet-smelling breath odor known as fetor hepaticus. The diagnosis is clinical, and the mainstay of treatment is the identification and treatment of precipitating factors. Pharmacologic treatments are targeted at the reduction of ammonia production in the GI tract and include lactulose and nonabsorbable antibiotics. Incorrect Options: Option A - The serum ammonia level correlates with the severity of hepatic encephalopathy: There is a poor correlation between ammonia levels and disease severity. Option B - The diagnosis is made by electroencephalograph: Hepatic encephalopathy is primarily a clinical diagnosis. Option D - TIPS placement is a second-line treatment: TIPS placement is a common cause of hepatic encephalopathy. In some patients with post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy, reduction or occlusion of the shunt may help control symptoms that are refractory to pharmacologic measures. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Discharge the patient on NSAIDS, warm compresses, and antibiotics by mouth, and refer for outpatient follow up in 2-3 days: The patient has superficial thrombophlebitis from an IV insertion. In these cases, there is rarely a workup needed. Unless it appears that the involved area is extensive, there is no indication for anticoagulation . This patient is low risk for developing DVT, so discharge with NSAIDs for pain, warm compresses to reduce swelling, and antibiotics to cover the small area of cellulitis before close outpatient follow up is appropriate. Incorrect Options: Option A - Admit the patient for IV vancomycin, start heparin, and obtain right upper extremity ultrasound: Intravenous antibiotics, anticoagulation, and a right upper extremity ultrasound is not indicated in the absence of fevers or other signs of infection or sepsis, extensive area of involvement, or clinical suspicion for DVT. Option B - Obtain right arm ultrasound and discharge on low molecular weight heparin, coumadin, and antibiotics: Discharge on two anticoagulants after an ultrasound for superficial thrombophlebitis is inappropriate. The cost, inconvenience, and risk of anticoagulation for a patient without identifiable risk factors for DVT should not be the initial management. Among others, important risk factors for DVT include varicose veins, previous history of thrombosis or stroke, heart failure, chronic lung disease, and smoking. Her left arm and left leg are twitching frequently and display greatly increased tone. She has left facial twitching as well and although she has no aphasia, she has mild garbled speech. She has no focal weakness and can lift both arms and legs equally. What should you do for this patient?

questions.solution: Correct Option B - She needs immediate IV lorazepam: She is in epilepsia partialis continua, or a form of status epilepticus with simple partial seizures. In this case the sensorium is clear and there is not generalized movement. The arm and leg are the most commonly affected. As in other seizures , benzodiazepines like lorazepam are the first-line choice to break it. A CT and labs need to be checked in her case since they are new onset, but breaking the seizure and maintaining the airway are what is imperative initially. Incorrect Options: Option A - She is having a complicated ischemic stroke and needs a stat CT of the brain and likely should get IV TPA: A stroke would be characterized by a motor deficit, not by movement. Option C - She is displaying pseudoseizure behavior and needs a psych consult: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures are not associated with physiological central nervous system dysfunction. Clues that may help with diagnosis include long duration, fluctuating course, asynchronous movements, pelvic thrusting, ictal eye closing or crying, memory recall, side-to-side head or body movements, and absent postictal confusion. Option D - Even though her FS is normal, she may be relatively hypoglycemic and needs a bolus of D-50: Hypoglycemia would present with physiologic signs, including tremor, palpitations, and catecholamine or acetylcholine mediated effects, including anxiety and arousal, sweating, and paresthesias. questions.solution: Correct Option B - 1: The CURB-65 is a criteria used to identify patients who can be managed as outpatients or inpatients. It is also used as a severity score to predict mortality due to community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). It consists of 5 variables; each scored 1 point. These include: New-onset confusion Urea > 7mmol/L Respiratory rate > 30/min Systolic blood pressure (SBP)< 90mmHg or diastolic blood pressure (DBP)< 60mmHg Age > 65 years As this patient had no confusion, urea <7mmol/L, SBP<90mmHg, DBP<60mmHg, is below 65 years of age, and respiratory rate of 31, the CURB-65 totals up to 1. Patients with a score of 0-1 can be treated as outpatients. Patients with a score of 2 require hospital-supervised treatment. It can be a short-stay inpatient or hospital-supervised outpatient treatment. Patients with a score of 3 or more should be managed for severe pneumonia in the hospital. Patients with a score of 4 and 5 require intensive care treatment. Incorrect Options: Option A - 0: The CURB-65 score for this patient cannot be 0 as the respiratory rate is more than 30/min, giving it a score of 1. Option C - 2: The patient meets no variable other than the respiratory rate to fulfil the CURB-65 criteria; hence the score cannot exceed 1. Option D - 3: The patient meets no variable other than the respiratory rate to fulfil the CURB-65 criteria; hence the score cannot exceed 1. @Neet_pg_bot

Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory disease characterized by the irreversible dilation and thickening of the bronchial walls due to recurrent infections, inflammation, or obstruction. This leads to the accumulation of mucus and impaired clearance, leading to recurrent lung infections and chronic cough. The dilation of bronchi can be seen in imaging studies like chest X-rays, CT scans, or bronchograms Incorrect Options: Option B - Increased numbers of alveoli in the lungs: Increased numbers of alveoli in the lungs is not a morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis because Bronchiectasis is a condition that primarily affects the bronchi, which are the large airways that lead from the trachea to the lungs Alveoli are small air sacs within the lungs where gas exchange occurs. They are not directly affected by Bronchiectasis, although if the condition is severe and chronic, it can eventually damage the alveoli and other lung structures. The primary morphological characteristics of Bronchiectasis are related to the bronchial walls, including dilation, thickening, and scarring. Option C - Presence of fluid-filled cavities in the lungs: Presence of fluid-filled cavities in the lungs is not a defining morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis. Cysts or cavities are sometimes observed in patients with Bronchiectasis, but this is not always true. Option D - Presence of nodules in the lungs: Presence of nodules in the lungs is not a defining morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis. Therefore, in patients with impaired kidney function (creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min), dose adjustments are necessary to prevent drug accumulation and potential side effects. Instead, deruxtecan is a complex antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) in which deruxtecan is linked to the monoclonal antibody Trastuzumab, which targets HER2-positive breast cancer cells. questions.stem: A 40-year-old sailor is transported to a military treatment facility 20 minutes after being engaged in a navy ship collision. He feels the need to defecate but is unable to do so. He appears to be sick. The pulse rate is 140 beats per minute; respirations are 28 beats per minute, and blood pressure is 104/70 mm Hg. Ecchymosis over the scrotum and perineum is found during a pelvic examination. There is tenderness over the suprapubic area and blood at the urethral meatus. A high-riding prostate is revealed by digital rectal examination. An abdominal ultrasound reveals a mildly distended bladder. X-rays of the sacrum reveal fractures in all four pubic rami. Which of the following is the most probable cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old sailor is transported to a military treatment facility 20 minutes after being engaged in a navy ship collision. He feels the need to defecate but is unable to do so. A high-riding prostate is revealed by digital rectal examination. An abdominal ultrasound reveals a mildly distended bladder. X-rays of the sacrum reveal fractures in all four pubic rami. Which of the following is the most probable cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Tearing of posterior urethra Inability to urinate despite desire, suprapubic pain, blood at the urethral meatus, scrotal and perineal ecchymoses, and a high-riding prostate are all symptoms of torn posterior urethra, all of which are present in this patient. The posterior urethra's membranous section is most vulnerable to damage from high-risk pelvic injuries. Therefore, a torn posterior urethra is consistent with the patient's trauma report and the x-ray results (fractures of all four pubic rami). To prove urethral injury, this patient should have a retrograde cystourethrogram. Placing a Foley catheter before conducting a urethrogram should be avoided because it could exacerbate the injury. Catheterization shouldn't be done [ if blood is found at meatus] - Partial tear may get converted to complete tear(but in case of small partial tear, a single gentle attempt of catheterization with smallest catheter can be done) Incorrect options: Option B: Rupture of the bladder Bladder rupture is a complication of high-risk pelvic fractures that can result in urinary retention and suprapubic pain. However, due to the absence of urethral involvement, a bladder perforation would not account for the patient's blood at the meatus and high-riding prostate on physical examination. Furthermore, an ultrasound would not reveal a dilated bladder and patients usually present with gross hematuria. Option C: Rupture of corpous cavernosum Traumatic bowing to erect penis results in a rupture of the tunica albuginea of the corpus cavernosum, which leads to penile fracture. When a penile fracture and urethral damage coexist, the penile hematoma or blood at the meatus may result. However, on physical examination, the patient's failure to void, scrotal, and perineal ecchymoses, or high-riding prostate could not be attributed to a penile fracture. Additionally, this kind of damage usually happens during sexual activity. Option D: Blunt trauma to the prostate The patient's appearance is unlikely to be due to blunt trauma to the prostate. Physical examination may reveal a high-riding prostate, failure to urinate, blood at the meatus, scrotal and perineal ecchymoses, and other symptoms associated with high-risk pelvic injuries (fractures of all four pubic rami). However, these results are not related to blunt trauma to the prostate gland itself. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Option D: Doppler echocardiography Echocardiography is a crucial study for patients with aortic stenosis suspicions. Doppler evaluation enables the computation of the systolic gradient across the aortic valve, using which the severity of stenosis can be determined. Doppler echocardiography is the gold standard for assessing the severity of aortic stenosis, as it allows for calculating the systolic gradient across the aortic valve. This is important because the stenosis's severity determines the patient's appropriate management. It can accurately measure the pressure gradient across the aortic valve and calculate the aortic valve area using various formulas (e.g., continuity equation, Gorlin equation). In this instance, the patient had significant aortic stenosis with an aortic valve area of 0.6 cm 2 and a peak velocity of 4.5 m/s, indicating the necessity for precise evaluation of stenosis severity. Furthermore, Doppler echocardiography can examine the function of the left ventricle, the degree of aortic regurgitation, and the existence of concomitant valve lesions, all crucial variables in selecting the therapeutic strategy for aortic stenosis. Option A: Coronary angiography Coronary angiography is unsuitable for assessing the severity of aortic stenosis. Coronary angiography is an imaging test used to visualize the coronary arteries to identify blockages or narrowing that may cause chest pain or a heart attack. It lacks information regarding the severity of aortic stenosis. Coronary angiography is used to assess the confirmation of coronary artery-related pathology, which could be a coexisting condition. However, it is not the most appropriate test to evaluate the severity of aortic stenosis. Option B: CT angiography CT angiography is an imaging procedure that utilizes X-rays and computer technology to produce images of the heart and blood vessels in exquisite detail. Although it may be beneficial for determining the degree of valve calcification in aortic stenosis, it is not the method of choice for determining the severity of stenosis itself. CT angiography can provide information about valve calcification but does not accurately assess stenosis severity. Although coronary angiography may be recommended in patients with aortic stenosis who exhibit symptoms suggestive of coronary artery disease, it is not the test of choice to determine the severity of aortic stenosis Option C: Exercise stress testing Exercise stress testing is generally not advised for patients with severe aortic stenosis, as it can raise the risk of further cardiovascular events such as syncope, angina, and sudden death. In such instances, exercise stress testing will likely yield less relevant information.
